question: Are calories just calories? Is it the same if you get a calorie from a fizzy drink or a piece of fruit or a slice of potato or a bit of cheese?
answer: A calorie is a physical measure of energy - specifically, the amount of energy needed to heat one metric mililitre of water by one degree Celsius. Energy in food intake is also measured in this way, though the terms kilocalorie and calorie are often used interchangably, which can cause confusion.  But yes, no matter where it comes from, one calorie always represents the exact same amount of energy. However, a difference you *can* make is that some foods will allow the energy that is within them to be absorbed more efficiently or more quickly, which can lead to varying results. (Edit courtesy of Neo6874: One calorie heats one millilitre by one degree Celsius. One kilocalorie heats one litre by one degree Celsius.)

question: Why is it my jaw (below the ear) hurts after I blow up a balloon that's tough to inflate?
answer: The eustachian tube is what is hurting; it was stretched by the air pressure used to inflate the balloon, and is sore.  The reason it feels like it is coming from your jaw below the ear, is a phenomenon called *referred pain*. The same nerve branch that brings pain signals to your brain from your jaw, there, is the same branch that brings pain signals from your eustachian tube. The eustachian tube is so rarely in pain that the brain never learned to differentiate between the two sources, and so interprets pain from it, as being pain from your jaw instead. Referred pain happens often, usually in cases of sinus pain, toothaches, and abdominal pain. It can also happen in heart attacks, where the person experiencing the heart attack feels pain in their left arm instead of their chest.

question: What is a homeowners association and why can't they give you orders on what your house/garden should look like?
answer: HOAs are typically started by a developer who owns a big group of properties they're selling off. Essentially, when anyone buys a house in their development, they agree to join and abide by the HOA as a part of their purchase contract. Once a certain number of homes are sold, the developer typically turns the HOA over to the directors, who are generally home owners in the area. The purpose from the developer's viewpoint is to prevent people who have recently bought into a community from doing anything annoying or stupid that will make the remainder of the homes more difficult to sell. Home owners tend to like them because it prevents their neighbors from doing anything annoying or stupid that will bring down their property value. They are controversial because they are not a government body, can be undemocratic, occasionally enable abuse by the directors, and basically levy a second property tax.

question: Why do different foods of the same mass have different amounts of calories?
answer: Your body isn't converting all the mass of a burger into energy lol. Only some of the energy bound up in food is utilized by your body, and none of it comes from converting mass into energy. Your body takes chemical potential energy from bonds between atoms in your food and (after generally storing that energy in different chemical bonds) utilizes it to drive all the processes that keep you alive. Much of the actual mass of the food is used as raw material to make structures your body needs like new cells etc. Some of that material is used wholesale because your body can't produce it on its own (like vitamins). Any mass your body can't use generally leaves the body with other waste. Some food has more, and more energetic, bonds that your body is capable of converting into energy than others.

This will cause diarrea and causes dehydration. Some ingredients work as a diuretic, which means you will pee more because of them. Think of beer and coffee. While uptake may be the same as with normal water (but probably isn't the same) you also excrete more of it. So, the additional ingredients do matter.

question: Why isn't a Bluetooth connection instant?
answer: Whenever two electronic devices talk to each other they go through what's called a "handshake" - basically it's the two devices trying to negotiate a common ground and make sure they can continue speaking in a stable fashion.  > Device A: "Hey! Hey is anyone there?"  > Device B: "Yeah, I'm here. Hi, I'm B. Wanna talk?"  > Device A: "Hey B. Yeah I want to talk... I'm on Bluetooth v. 2 and can talk at 2.1Mbit/s, how about you?"  > Device B: "oooh... no I can't do that... I'm on Bluetooth v. 1.2 and can only talk at .7Mbit/s, is that ok?"  > Device A: "Yeah that's not a problem I can handle that. Ok so we'll use v1.2 and talk at .7Mbit/s, deal?"  > Device B: "Deal."  > Devices are now officially connected.

question: Why is disinfecting wounds painful?
answer: There's two main reasons. First, the wound is sensitive, as that part of the body has been damaged and is screaming at your brain to start taking damage control steps. Putting anything in an open wound is going to hurt some. Second, the things we use to disinfect typically do that by killing biological material, which will include the cells around and in your wound. So basically you're quarantining and nuking the area to make sure the infection doesn't spread. The basic part of your brain that handles pain doesn't understand that, or the reasons for disinfection, it just sees more damage to an already damaged part of the body, and registers it as pain.

question: Why do many R-rated movies only show quick flashes of nudity?
answer: Film rating and classification groups (like the MPAA) take into account the duration of nudity when establishing an appropriate rating for a movie.  Extended nudity (especially if the nudity is sexualized or presented in a sexual context) may result in a higher film rating classification (e.g. NC-17 in the US). Thus the nudity is presented relatively briefly (not in a pornographic way) as to keep the rating R or below. Movie studios are very concerned about getting films rated NC-17 because it is very hard to make money when a film receives this rating. This is partly due to restrictions on advertising for NC-17 films, but also because many theaters and retail outlets will refuse to show and sell (respectively) NC-17 movies. Note that brief non-sexual depictions of nudity can appear in films rated as low as PG, but most films depicting explicit nudity (e.g. bare breasts) are unlikely to receive ratings lower than PG-13 and in most cases will be rated R.

question: How come we can multiply by zero, but we can't divide by it?
answer: It helps to think about what division actually means. If I write, say, 6 ÷ 3 = 2, what do I mean by that? Well, I mean that, if you multiply 2 by 3, you'll get 6. In other words, 6 ÷ 3 represents "the number that, when multiplied by 3, gives you 6". Obviously there is only one such number. But with zero, you run into trouble. Zero times anything is still zero, so if I write something like 6 ÷ 0 ("the number that, when multiplied by 0, gives you 6") there is no number that does the job. And if I write 0 ÷ 0, *every* number does the job. Multiplying by zero "forgets" information about what you multiplied by, and thus cannot be undone by division.

question: What is sound? And why is it made?
answer: Sound is how our brains interpret vibrations in the air. When you tap the table, it causes the table, your finger, and the air around it, to briefly vibrate. question: Why is it more tiring to stand than to walk?

question: Why does changing my position on the scale change my weight?
answer: In a simple scale, the force is only measured at a single point. If your center of mass is over that point, you get an accurate measure. However, as you move your center of mass away from that point, you're applying two different forces - a downward force and a lateral force. Only the downward component of that force is actually measured by the scale. Think of a playground seesaw. You probably weigh a good deal more than your 3-year-old son. But you can 'balance' the seesaw if your 3-year-old sits at the very end of the seesaw while you sit almost on top of the fulcrum. In such a situation, nearly the entire force of your son's weight would be downward while most of your weight would be exerting a lateral force rather than a downward one.

question: Why does a finger or a stylus work on a touch screen but other items (like a glove) do not?
answer: So most modern touchscreens work by something called capacitance. Capacitance relates to how well an object can hold an electric charge. There's this thing (which I believe is called a matrix, and there's actually two of them, but that's not important for this) behind the screen on your phone (or tablet or laptop or whatever it is) that holds a very small electric charge, and when your finger gets close to it, a tiny bit of that charge moves to your finger, and away from the device. The device can detect that small drop in charge and figure out where you're touching the screen. The reason a glove or other things don't work on the touch screen is because they have very poor capacitance and won't take that extra charge as easily as a finger or stylus will.

question: Why doesn't inbreeding work out in the long run?
answer: > Natural selection should get rid of deleterious alleles This is exactly why inbreeding causes problems. Recessive alleles that are deleterious can "hide" from natural selection in heterozygous individuals (people with one dominant allele and one recessive allele). Inbreeding increases the chances that an individual will inherit two recessive deleterious alleles (because the chance that both their parents will carry the same deleterious alleles is increased if they're related). If the deleterious effect on fitness is high enough, that person will not reproduce. If it's only mild then they may reproduce, but maybe not as much, or they're children might also not be very fit. The point is that inbreeding exposes recessive deleterious alleles to natural selection thus allowing them to *possibly* be removed from the population as a whole. In the mean time, those people who are the products of inbreeding suffer from the deleterious effects.

Graveyards are usually owned by the church or local council so profit is not a factor.

question: Why can Social Security "run out" whereas programs like Welfare cannot?
answer: "Running out" is a bit misleading. Most people will get money pulled each paycheck to go towards Social Security, so assuming the system doesn't change, there will always be something to pay out to retirees. What can run out, though, is the Social Security Trust Fund. For a while now, Social Security has taken in more money than its paid out, and the excess has been put into the Trust Fund. We're hitting the point, though, where the money coming in from Social Security taxes is less than what's being paid out, which is what the Trust Fund is for, to make up the difference. The way it's looking, eventually the Trust Fund will be used up, so there won't be anything to cover the shortfall. But again, there will still be money coming in, so Social Security will still pay out something, just not as much as promised. Unless, of course, the system gets changed to prevent that. It's happened before, and old people vote.

Once the baby is born, this kinocilium is no longer needed, and it involutes. Turns out hair cells only begin working optimally once their kinocilium has fully involuted. Guess what? Involution occurs first in hair cells tuned to high pitches, going in step-wise order down to the hair cells tuned to low pitches. Furthermore, myelination of neurons in the auditory nerve also occurs first in neurons carrying information about high-pitched frequencies. Thus, babies should hear and respond better to higher-pitched sounds, until the rest of their hair cells and auditory neurons mature.

question: How do "sick days" in the US work?
answer: There's no laws in the US that grant everyone vacation time, sick time, paid days off or any of that so exactly what a "sick day" means is entirely up to the individual company's policies. Generally, a sick day is considered a *benefit* - something the company isn't required to give you but agrees to. It (usually) means that you can call in sick, on short notice, as being unable to work & still get paid. What happens if you're sick & you've used all your sick days (or never had any to begin with) also depends on the company. In many states, a business would be within their rights to fire you for not wanting to come into work on a day you're expected to be there, regardless of the reason. Most companies would let you take the day off, without pay, if you give them enough advance notice, provided you don't do it *too* often (in which case, you're fired). If you work someplace that also gives you paid vacation days (which not all companies do), they might let you use your vacation days as sick days.

question: What is actually happening when a CD or DVD is burned?
answer: A laser is shined onto the surface to cause a small burned spot on the disc. This is done very rapidly as the disc spins, giving a dot pattern in a very tight spiral from the inside of the disc to the outer edge. Later, a lower-powered laser can be shined onto those spots and a detector can look for a reflection. Seeing a reflection means a 1; no reflection means a 0, or vice-versa if that's the way the format is defined. Rewritable CDs and DVDs are similar, but instead of irreversibly burning a spot on the disc they strike a bit of cool material that can either be in a crystalline (all atoms lined up in rows) or amorphous (all atoms in randomly aligned locations) states. Hitting this material with a laser can cause it to change, and only one of the states is reflective, thus allowing the same general principle to be used to read them.

question: Why can we move all of our fingers independently of each other minus our ring finger?
answer: It's all about training. Your brain takes as many shortcuts as possible when it's learning how to move all of your limbs and is happy to lose ability if you don't use it. This is why physical therapy is so important after an accident or surgery: your brain can develop shortcuts that make things easier in the short run, but harder in the long run. People who work with their hands (pianists, artists, martial arts practitioners) can learn to move each finger independently and make use of that range of movement. Otherwise, your brain doesn't see the need to keep the extra neurons dedicated to that task and reassigns them to more important work.

question: Why are forest fires considered good for the forest?
answer: For almost 100 years, the common forest management theory was exactly the same as yours. Stop all fires in the forests. The problem was when fires broke out they were more intense and more damaging than they should have been. The current theory is regular low intensity fires are good for the over all forest health. Fires burn up dead and unhealthy trees which may be harboring diseases, beetles, termites, etc which will spread and weaken healthy trees.  Fires clear out the undergrowth such as bushes and smaller trees which act as ladders to help the fire spread to the canopy of the tree. With out a thick undergrowth the trees survive. Fires burn up the leaf litter on the forest floor and help return the nutrients to the soil. Finally some trees need the heat of a fire to open their pine cones, or other seeds.

question: what is FPTP voting and why is bad?
answer: "First past the post voting" is a system where the candidate who receives a plurality in a district takes the single seat for that district. It's not bad, but like any voting system, it has its pros and cons. An upside is that you have a lot of influence on the individual that gets elected, and you have a direct connection to him--he's *your* representative, rather than just being one of many national legislators. (Contrast the common implementation of proportional voting, where there are no districts and you only vote for parties, not individuals.) The commonly named downside is that minorities that are spread out over each district may not be reflected in the legislature--10% of the national population might support party X, but if they are not a plurality anywhere they'll get 0% of the seats. I'm afraid I'm not familiar with Canada's particular reform plans.

question: How did saluting start? and when?
answer: Pretend you are a knight, in armor. You have a helmet, with a visor. You are approached by your lord, so you lift your visor so that he can see who he is speaking to. Make that motion with your hand - it is a lot like saluting. The same goes for tipping one's hat, a common courtesy that continued well after the Middle Ages. This is the likely origin of the salute. When it precisely started is unknown, but I'd put my money on the late Middle Ages, when visor helmets were quite common. Even before the modern salute was created, displaying one's right arm was a common gesture throughout many cultures. Why? Well, most people are right-handed, meaning that most people would use weapons with their right hands. Displaying that one's hand was not on a weapon was a sign of peace.

question: Why do Public Domain books cost money on app stores?
answer: If a work is public domain, anyone can take it and charge money for it. Night of the Living Dead is a good example. It's public domain work now, anyone can make a DVD of it and sell it in stores.  Most free public domain ebooks are actually scanned and distrusted by volunteers who feel the work should accessible for free for everyone. A larger company may see the same book and charge for it because of a variety of reasons. Maybe their edition has some editorials. Maybe it's got pictures and diagrams. Or maybe they just figure that if they charge for it, someone will buy it even if there's a free version. The interesting thing about public domain work is that you can buy a copy and then distribute it yourself. Completely legal.

question: Why is it that characters in video games often have difficulty to directly touch each other?

Most animation systems rely on some kind of 'skeleton' of sorts as a basis for movement, and then use distances from that skeleton to determine if something hit that character. (That's an oversimplification of sorts, but this is ELI5 so bear with me). This allows others to interact with the "surface" of the 'model' (i.e. touch the outer part of the body somehow). It's fine for an arrow because that's a simple two-dimensional (maybe curved a little) path. But it's not for a handshake where the amount of math required to make one hand fit properly inside another and then grasp and squeeze and fold fingers and skin is pretty daunting. Getting that perfect is going to take a super-big lot of testing tweaking and adjustments, and enough players will let it go that it's not worth delaying a game's release date.

question: Why do we still use BC and AD terminologies?
answer: So, in the original terminology, AD stands for Anno Domini (Year of our Lord) and BC stands for Before Christ. The newer terminology is CE (Common Era) and BCE (Before common era). The old one is still used more just because it's the convention, and most non-Christians don't care enough to really try to change it. The problem with "adding" is that, for one, where do we count from? The earth was formed billions of years ago, and even when civilization rolled around more recently, there aren't a lot of hard dates we can nail down. Also, most people don't really have a hard time understanding the difference between AD and BC. To change it, you'd basically have to rewrite every history book and change the dates to the new standard. That's a lot of effort, for really no benefit.

question: If you have a no trespassing sign, in what situations can you legally shoot a trespasser?
answer: > If you have a no trespassing sign, in what situations can you legally shoot a trespasser? In general, if you sincerely believe that your life (or the life of another) is in danger, and you (or they) will die (or be seriously injured) if you don't shoot. Some jurisdictions in the US have "duty to retreat" laws that say that you have to try to escape, and can only use deadly force if escape is not an option. Other jurisdictions have "stand your ground" laws that don't required you to try to flee, but also don't let you kill someone unless there is a real and imminent threat to your life (or, in some cases, your property) In no circumstance are you allowed to shoot someone *just* for trespassing, no matter what your sign says.

question: What is a "housing bubble," and what can cause it to burst?
answer: A housing bubble happens when the demand for houses is far greater than the supply which inflates prices as buyers compete with each other. If there are only 100 homes up for sale in an area and 5000 people willing to buy them a seller can ask significantly more for their home than someone in an area with 100 homes for sale and only 50 potential buyers. As prices increase, the number of potential buyers decrease. Eventually the market is full of homes that barely anybody can afford to buy and some of the people who bought at grossly inflated prices might no longer afford to pay back their loans and lose their homes to the bank. The sale price of homes starts to go down as people realize that they can no longer find people willing to buy houses at the prices they were asking.

As for banking it is illegal for banks to offer services to illegal businesses. So in Colorado where it is legal under state law and illegal under federal law banks generally still refuse business from marijuana dispensaries. They therefore either have to deal strictly in cash or open bank accounts under false pretenses and switch banks every time the bank's compliance department catches on.

question: Why is a Diesel vehicle more economical than a petrol version of the same vehicle?
answer: At a very basic level, diesel is more 'energy dense' than petrol, and the means by which it is ignited in the engine mean that, broadly, you can get more power per litre of fuel. The fuel is under a lot of pressure, and effectively ignites on it's own, which is why they don't need spark plugs (they use glow plug, which get things going initially, but once you're on your way the pressure of the cylinders is enough to make the fuel explode). This used to be the case, but with modern technology it's increasingly less so - That said, in a lot of the world it's just cheaper too (because it's less refined), though with rising fuel prices (the US is an outlier here) it's just less expensive!

question: Why is it that when you hear your voice in recordings you think you sound so different, yet everyone else thinks you sound the same?
answer: When you speak, vibrations from your vocal cords resonate in your throat and mouth, and some get transmitted and by the bones in your neck and head. The inner ear responds to these just like any other vibrations, turning them into electrical signals and sending them to the brain. Whenever you speak, your inner ear is stimulated both by internal vibrations in your bones and by the sound coming out of your mouth and traveling through the air and into the ears. This combination of vibrations coming to the inner ear by two different paths gives your voice (as you normally hear it) a unique character that other, “air only” sounds don’t have. In particular, your bones enhance deeper, lower-frequency vibrations and give your voice a fuller, bassier quality that’s lacking when you hear it on a recording.

question: Why is it that I can be extremely cold without a blanket, extremely hot with a blanket, but be just right with one foot hanging out?
answer: The part of your foot that is not under the blanket is acting like a radiator, shedding body heat and cooling the blood that circulates through it.  A similar effect can be had by hanging your feet in a cool stream on a hot day. Even though only a small amount of your skin is touching the water, your entire body can quickly cool down to comfortable levels due to the heat exchange and circulating blood flow.  Fun fact: Your body regulates the amount of heat loss through the skin by opening or closing thousands of tiny blood vessels located just beneath the surface of your skin. The "numb" feeling you get after plunging into freezing water is due to the blood vessels slamming closed in an attempt to save body heat. The red "flushed" appearance the skin gets in the heat is the opposite: the tiny vessels are wide open and attempting to lose as much heat as possible.

question: How is Linkedin worth $26 billion dollars, when it only has around $550 million in revenue per year?
answer: People that frequent LinkedIn are often the types that make business decisions. If you look at the people with the most "connections" on the site, they're usually fairly senior individuals with titles like Director or Manager or Vice President, and they quite often have a budget for making decisions associated with buying information technology.  So they are a perfect target market all lined up for a firm that sells software and cloud-based delivery services to advertise to. And since Microsoft now owns the site, they can populate it with their ads and reinforce their brand on it... and perhaps more importantly, prevent advertisers with competing products from advertising there as long as they don't get slapped for monopoly behaviour.  LinkedIn might not be worth much in terms of REVENUE, but it's worth an amazing amount in terms of concentrating business decision-makers. And access to them is what Microsoft paid for.

question: Is there anything ethically or legally wrong with starting a charity you don't care about to give yourself a job, assuming you pay yourself A fair salary and actually donate the money you raise?
answer: Legally no. Ethically, it depends on what sort of ethics you subscribe to. In our society utilitarian ethics are the most commonly used for day to day decisions, which state that the best outcome for the most people is the most ethical choice, regardless of how you achieve that outcome. In a utilitarian system, which again is what most people use to a greater or lesser extent, it would be ethical. In deontological ethics the action is more important than the outcome. In some ways why you do something is as important as how you do it. It would be very ethically iffy to start the charity for selfish reasons in a deontological ethical system even if it has overall positive outcomes. So, it depends on what form of ethics you subscribe to. I don't think it would be seen as overwhelmingly evil though to start a charity and do charitable work even if the reasons are somewhat selfish.

question: How do casinos prevent counterfeit chips. Why can't someone duplicate some chips and cash them in? It appear far simpler than cash.
answer: Counterfeit chips do happen, but there are some security measures in place to help prevent it. Microchips imbedded in the chips themselves, microprinted serial numbers, very precise branding and logos, and even the material composition is secret. The people who make these chips are the same companies that make checks and credit cards. All the high value chips have RFID sensors inside of them, too. And even if you could make a chip that was indistinguishable from one casino's chip, trying to turn them in would be very difficult. You'd have to smuggle them into the casino and cash them out at the cashier, but any large number of chips being cashed causes security to look through the security footage to determine if you got them legally. The RFID sensor tracks which table or game they came from, so it's very easy to check the cameras.

question: What is the "Half life" of something, Why is it important, and how do you figure it out?
answer: Something's half-life is the time it takes for half of that substance to decay into something else, whether through chemical or radioactive means. After one half-life, 50% of that substance is left. Then 25%, 12.5%, and so on. It is important because it gives you an idea of how long that substance will be around. For example, if a chemical has a half life of 100 days, and it's in the soil, that gives you an idea of how long it would take for the soil to be free of that chemical without intervention, which could have applications in crop management or pollution. Radioactive waste is another good example. You determine it mathematically by measuring the substance for a set period of time to determine how much of it decays.

answer: You lose your sense of taste when you're sick for the same reason you lose your sense of smell: your nose is clogged up! What we perceive as "flavor" is a mixture of smell and taste. This is why holding your nose when you eat makes foods that you don't like easier to handle. When you put food in your mouth and chew it, the smell is carried up through the back of your throat to your nasal passages. This is another reason why drinking wine while you eat enhances flavor. The alcohol in the wine evaporates, "picking up" the tiny molecules of food and lifting them up into your nasal passages, making it easier to perceive flavor in the food.

question: What is happening in my body when I get the feeling I'm hungry?
answer: A lot of the sensation of being hungry comes from your brain and not your stomach. You often feel hungry in response to changes in your blood sugar level rather than the fullness or emptyness of your stomach or intestines. When you actually do feel pain or discomfort from your abdomen while being hungry, that means that part of your stomach or intestines are actually empty of food and bile, but the involuntary muscular contractions that help you digest food are still taking place. A 'bubble' may actually be a pocket of gas from digesting starchy food being moved back and forth by these contractions. It may also be air you swallowed. Most of the time it's just your stomach or intestines writhing, though. Nice image, huh?

question: Why do computers get slower over time, even when there is lots of space left on the hard drive?
answer: If we're talking purely about hard drives, it's mainly due to fragmentation of the hard drive. If you imagine you have three files, created one after another, each file named numerically, they would slot in to places on the hard drive like so: |1|2|3| But then say you edited file one and made it twice the size, this addition would have to go on the end, in a new slot: |1|2|3|1| Your two bits of file one are now separate and hence take longer to access when using them. This can also happen when deleting files, say I deleted file two. You would end up with: |1| |3|1| And then when file one is made even bigger: |1(Part i) | 1(Part iii) |3| 1(Part ii)| This fragmentation can happen without you knowing and just by using the computer, as all programs and operations use files.

question: Japan adopts negative interest rates. Should everyone else worry?
answer: One way to understand negative interest rates is the fisher equation. The central bank creates an expected inflation of 5%, but sets the nominal interest rate at 1%. The difference between the two (inflation and nominal interest rate) is the real interest rate (r = i - infl.) Therefore in the case, the real interest rate is -4%. This means that the rate of inflation overtakes the return on holding money, so the real value of money depreciates. Theoretically, its supposed to encourage people to spend and invest their money instead of holding it in savings accounts. Whether it really works, I don't know.

question: What allows heat to cast a shadow?
answer: Light is bent or refracted by whatever it passes through. In a room of uniform temperature, the light is bent the same way everywhere so you see a uniform image. Heat causes turbulence in the air so the light is bent in a more chaotic manner. You're seeing this as a wavy image in the shadow. This is also what causes mirages and the wavy pattern that one can see on top of a car hood when the engine is hot. This happens not only to light, but any part of the electromagnetic spectrum. Radio signals are disrupted in the morning and the evening, thermal inversion. As the air quickly heats up or cools down, the radio waves are distorted by the same effect. Thus causing a distorted signal and static in the radio program you're listening to at those times.

question: What was the first thing that was used to define how long one second is?
answer: Clocks weren't accurate enough to measure time to the second until the 17th century. The first clocks to do this were pendulum clocks, which were first invented in 1656 by Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens. One second was defined as being equal to 1/86,400 of a mean solar day. This is easy to derive from the fact that there are 60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour, and 24 hours in a mean solar day. In 1956, the second was redefined in terms of a year rather than a day to make it more accurate. The new second was defined as the fraction ​1⁄31,556,925.9747 of the tropical year 1899 on December 31st at 12:00 (Epoch January 0 1900). Finally, in 1967, a second was redefined as exactly 9,192,631,770 cycles of the radiation produced by the transition between two levels of cesium 133, as measured using atomic clocks.

question: Why do so many countries have eagles on their coat of arms and where did it originate from?
answer: It originated with the Romans: the eagle was a powerful bird, and so came to represent the basic concept of power and authority. Later, various European royal families adopted the eagle, or something like it. Some of them, such as the Russian tsars, give the eagle two or sometimes even three heads. The Holy Roman Empire, a large collection of small states in central Europe (which very slowly evolved into modern Germany), used the eagle to represent the authority of the Empire over the individual states. When the United States was created, the Founding Fathers drew a lot of inspiration from Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome (which is why the *Senate* meets in the *Capitol*, for example), and so naturally adopted an eagle for the Great Seal of the United States -- although, of course, they were careful to use, instead of a generic European eagle, a specific species (the bald eagle) native to America.

Inbreeding is also a huge concern for zoos, with their small captive populations. Zoos keep pedigrees for lot of species bred in captivity, so they can avoid breeding related individuals with each other. You can see the consequences in pets if you think of purebred dogs, for example. Many dog breeds are likely to get specific medical issues, such as hip dysplasia in golden retrievers, due to many generations of inbreeding.

question: What makes a belly button an innie or an outie?
answer: The umbilical cord is cut at typically the same place for everyone, so this doesn't determine outtie versus innie. What happens for the average innie belly button is that the cord is cut, and the remainder of it shrivels up and falls off in level with the stomach. The child then develops more fat around the belly button and it levels off/"sinks in" to an innie. For an outtie, a longer piece of the umbilical cord "stays alive" rather than shriveling up and falling off, causing the belly button to protrude. The child still of course develops more fat, but since the piece of umbilical cord never died off, it is part of their skin. Instead of growing around it, it just grows with them.

question: Why is it that time feels slower while your dreaming?
answer: Its not the complete answer, but worth mentioning - when you dream, it's not necessarily progressing according to any time scale. The way our brains store memory is in large part based on scenarios and chains of events - instead of remembering a party like a movie, you remember discrete details (often vague) and how they fit together, then later your brain assembles these bits and pieces into very detailed (but occasionally incorrect) memories. The same thing goes on when you dream. If you dreamt about waiting an hour in a line somewhere, you didn't have to dream the full hour in sequence. All you needed to do was dream up the fact that it lasted an hour, and then later you remember it as such because that's how your memory of the dream was constructed.

question: Why do liquids damage electronics?
answer: Water, pure water, 100% pure water, is an insulator. It's also kind of dangerous, but that's another story. Water and most other liquids you're likely to spill on an an electronic has enough metal and conductive salts in it to bridge electrical circuitry. You're creating short circuits. Current where current isn't expected is going to result in micro and nano meter components to be damaged, and the salts will corrode components, too. There are plenty of fluids that are pretty inert. If you look around YouTube, you'll find computers entirely submerged in oils or exotic stuff like liquid nitrogen. So it's not everything that's bad.

question: Why do movie releases decide to use NR (not rated) instead of NC-17?
answer: The rating system is run by a committee that reviews and rates the film's based off of given items including--but not limited to--language, violence, sexual appropriateness, and subject matter. Film ratings have become such a prominent force in the success of a movie that directors and producers often change portions of their films to achieve a more marketable rating. The most successful is PG-13 with NC-17 the least. For that reason, some film makers opt to not have their film rated at all rather than reduce their work for the sake of a better rating. That in of itself is pretty much film suicide as well though. At least for movies looking for a large theatrical release. It's, at times, a controversial process. If you get the chance, watch the documentary This Film Is Not Yet Rated (it was on Netflix last I checked) which goes into detail about how the system works, how those in charge are abusing it, and even the sexism that occurs surprisingly often.

question: How did Black Friday start? Also why does it continue?
answer: Christmas shopping traditionally begins the day after Thankgiving, when all the sales begin. Many stores, even larger ones, make a significant portion of their yearly profits on the days on and after Black Friday. The term "Black Friday" came about in 1961 from Philadelphia police officers, who knew they would face much more work due to traffic jams, packed sidewalks, and mobbed stores. The media picked up on their usage, and the city attempted a campaign to change their usage to "Big Friday" (Obviously, not very successfully). The city's fight against the term only wound up spreading the use farther and wider than it had gone before, and "Black Friday" stuck.

This one of the biggest obstacles to massive spaceflight. A lot of that money is lost building a single-use rocket. A reusable rocket could conceivably cost much less.  The company developing the technology is going for space tourism, sending people into space for money, so this particular model can't really be used for sending things into permanent orbit, but perhaps that type of retro rocket technology could be used in future rocket designs to reduce the cost of sending payloads into space. We'd have to see. The idea behind the space shuttle was a reusable space vehicle, and it wasn't nearly as cost effective as NASA had hoped (lots of maintenance costs and longer than expected turn-around times that is, time between Mission A landing to Mission B launching).

question: What does the phrase "corporations are people" mean and why is it significant?
answer: "Corporations are people" is a legal fiction (that's not a derogatory term, it's just the name we use for the concept). What that means is that it's something that isn't technically true, but legally we pretend it's true because it makes things easier. We do this so that we can apply existing laws to new scenarios that may not have existed when the original laws were created. We allow corporations to "be people" legally so we can treat that as such for the purpose of enforcing contracts, and so that they can sue and be sued as if the were a person. More recently corporate personhood has been a political issue because of recent court cases involving corporations rights with respect to political speech.

Many Americans believe that someone who is less fortunate should work hard to achieve social mobility rather than benefit from government programs funded by tax payers who are were able to achieve success. That's not to say all Americans feel this way. A vast majority of Americans approve many social welfare programs.  Also, although OP defines his/her country as socialist, I suspect it is a country currently run by a socialist party, and not necessarily a socialist country. Using a Marxist-Leninist definition of socialism, Cuba and China barely even qualify as socialist. Unless the means of production are owned by the state (or cooperatively by the citizens), your country is not socialist, OP (even if it says so in your constitution).

question: What is the difference between forward and reverse osmosis?
answer: In osmosis, water travels through a membrane from a low-concentration (i.e. less dissolved solids) mixture to a high-concentration mixture until the concentration on both sides is the same. This happens spontaneously and can be quite dramatic if one side is extremely highly concentrated. This is why drinking salt water is so harmful, osmotic pressure starts sucking water out of your cells. *Reverse* osmosis is the inverse process, forcing water to cross from the concentrated side to the pure side. This *won't* happen naturally and requires high pressures, but also acts as a very effective filtration process because the membrane excludes most particulates and large ions.

question: How was the second invented
answer: A second is the *second* split of an hour, divided into sixtieths. First you have an hour, which you divide into sixty parts, the minutes, and dividing each of those parts into sixty new parts results in a second. The reason why its divided by 60 and not some other number like 10 is because the system has its roots in ancient civilization like the Babylonians, who used 60 as a base instead of 10 like we do. 60 might seem like a random number, but it isn't. It has very many divisors - 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30 and 60 itself. It makes for a pretty natural and sensible number base to play around with when it comes to math and commerce.

question: Why do we call handmade cooking "From scratch"?
answer: "From scratch" is an idiom that means "starting at zero" or "starting with the very basics". Here, it means cooking something from ingredients that haven't been heavily processed -- e.g. making your own sauce instead of buying a ready-made sauce mix. The original "scratch" was a mark in the gound at the beginning of a race. Some competitors might be given a head start as a handicap; those who didn't had to "start from scratch", i.e. they had to start from the line. There are references of starting races "from scratch" going back to the 19th century; by the mid-19th century it was being used in billiards to mean "start without a handicap" even though there wasn't a literal scratch to start from (it was now being used as a metaphor), and by 1918 it was being used in all senses to mean "start from nothing".

question: How does sandboxing (computer security) work?
answer: Say you are hosting a fancy dinner party in your back yard and your sister brought one of your nephews along. This young child needs to do something to be entertained but you really don't want them bothering your other guests. So what you do is give them a sandbox to play in. They can do whatever in the sandbox but they aren't allowed to leave or access anything outside the box without using standard methods. They can ask for juice but not cake. In computer security it is much the same idea, where applications are given a set of resources to use and standard methods of interaction. They are not allowed to do whatever they want in order to prevent misbehavior.

question: Why is it that evidence gained using unlawful means/without permission inadmissible in court even though that piece of evidence would make the person/company guilty?
answer: This is an intentional feature. The United States Constitution protects citizens against unreasonable search and seizure--if you could use evidence from illegal searches, there would be very little incentive to stick to legal ones. A key piece of evidence might well be worth the compensation you'd have to pay in a civil suit. That makes the protection meaningless. The only practical way to discourage the government from such behavior is to remove the benefit. To get a conviction, the prosecution has to "play by the rules," as it were. Now, do note that this only applies to bad acts by the government. If a random burglar breaks into your house, finds incriminating evidence and turns it over to the police, it's admissible. After all, there would be no government misconduct being penalized if the evidence was excluded in that case.

question: What makes Guns and Roses NOT Glam metal/Hair Metal?
answer: They are. Sort of. Glam metal (every metal sub-genre, really) revolves around a central lyrical theme: in the case of glam, it was partying, girls, drugs, sex, alcohol, motorcycles, riches, coke, love, mischievousness, etc. Guns 'n Roses played to this theme, but inverted it by displaying the grittier underbelly of it all: the "unglamorous" side of living for booze, drugs, and women: addiction, violence, insolvency, prostitution, homelessness, murder, love lost, and so on. They took "glam" and flipped it on its head. They took a genre known for being flamboyant, polished, colorful, and "fake", and showed something dirty, raw, and "real". I consider them "glam", at least derived from it, but in a way they were "grunge" before grunge became a thing. (FWIW, Skid Row did basically the same thing, around the same time. An underrated band, IMO).

question: Between Coke and Diet Coke, which is truly better for you and why?
answer: The general consensus is that neither is actually good for you and you'd be better off drinking water. But that's not what you asked, so which one would be less damaging? The biggest distinction is that regular soda has high fructose corn syrup (HFCS) and diet soda has aspartame. HFCS is pretty much just regular sugar. Its biggest drawback is that it contributes calories, which can lead to diabetes, weight gain and all the health problems associated with being too heavy. Aspartame is newer, so it's still being studied. Some of the research suggests that it can mess with how your body reacts to sugar, leading to increased sugar cravings later. I've also read a study suggesting that aspartame, like sugar, is associated with diabetes later in life. Unfortunately, there's no definitive answer at the moment.

question: Why does it take 3 business days for a bank to process an external transaction?
answer: Because they batch them nightly. Every night, the banks communicate every transaction, such as "Bill at ABank pays 50 to Bob at BBanak, Paul at BBank pays 40 to Peter at ABank", and so forth. The computers all look at the transactions and make sure they are OK, rejecting anything that might need a human to look at it. Then they work out how much money they need to send to each other ($10 to BBank in my example). Next day (the second day) people examine any transactions the computers didn't process, and, if they match up, they OK them. Then they go into that night's batch, and the money can then be credited to the recipient some time on the third day, depending on the bank's internal procedures. As they can't be sure that your transaction will go through on the nod on the first night, they quote '3 business days' to be sure they'll make that deadline.

question: If cancer is just cells mutating and dividing without abandon, how does it cause the "rot" we see in later stages?
answer: The cancerous "rot" you show below is a result of necrosis where the tumor has grown so much that it no longer get nutrients and oxygen from the blood supply. The cells on the interior of the tumor die. There are two types of cell death: apopotosis, which is tightly regulated, and necrosis, which is unregulated. Unregulated dying, as is the case in tumor rot, causes a cell to release all of its contents onto neighboring cells, causing those cells to necrose as well. This usually results in the entire area to start decomposing, causing secondary bacterial infections and general gross-ness. This is part of the reason why people with necrotising fasciitis (flesh eating disease) have to get entire areas of necrosis removed, like arms or legs or whatever to prevent the rot from spreading. Fortunately, in humans cancer rarely gets so bad that you see that extent of rot. Usually the tumor is palpable and can be treated or removed before huge rotting occurs. Source: PhD in cancer metabolism.

question: Why is there such a loud sound when we clap?
answer: You're compressing the air between your hands rapidly, creating a pressure wave. Which is, you know, what sound is. The best, loudest claps involve cupping your hands to trap more air between them. Your hands squeeze that air together before it rapidly expands again out through the gaps between your hands. That rapid compression and expansion is the sound wave that your ears detect. The more air you compress, the faster you compress it, and the harder you compress it, the louder the sound will be. Compare that to, say, clapping with wide open hands, palm against palm, and you won't get much of a sound, not matter how hard you clap, especially if you can get the heel of one palm into the center of the other so very very little air is trapped. You'll get a smacking sound, but that's mostly the sound of your skin smacking and vibrating the air, rather than a good solid compression of air like in a proper clap.

question: How can Amazon have a P/E ratio of 1k and have it be sustainable?
answer: There are several options.  1. It's not, and the price will decline, though be aware that the market can remain irrational longer than you can remain solvent.  2. The firm's earnings are temporarily impaired and when they recover the P/E will be substantially lower (this frequently occurs in highly cyclical businesses like semiconductor equipment). Investors price the business on profits over a cycle rather than a single year.  3. The firm is expected to grow rapidly, and at some point the growth results in massive profits. While a few firms sustain this sort of profit growth over 10-15 years (Google and Apple both achieved this level of sustained income growth from 2005 to 2015 but it's rather rare). So, investors expect a radical change in Amazon's earnings. Investors have a *long* history of being overwhelmingly optimistic, so if enough change their mind, the price will likely decline at some point.

question: How do laboratories find out what chemical that random sample is?
answer: They have plenty of methods. Let's go with gas chromatography: Vaporize your liquid and inject it into a gas chromatograph (a long column coated with an inert substance). The test substance moves through the column, interacting with the inert coating, causing the various chemicals inside it to separate out (as some "stick" to the coating and move slowly through it, while others just flow right through).  A detector at the end senses when each component comes through, and compares the time with the time of other chemicals on a database (for example, chemical x took 7.03 seconds to emerge, which matches up with chemical A on the database - therfore x is A).  It's not 100% accurate, since some chemicals will take 7.031 seconds and others 7.029, so if both are present, one will "hide" behind the other and it'll be difficult to distinguish between them. But the guys who do this are pretty smart, so they'd figure chemical x is more likely to be carbon than uranium (using completely random examples there).

question: Why video quality is based off a full circle's degrees. 360p, 720p, 1080p, 1440p, etc.
answer: Base video quality standards for a long time was approx 320 x 240 (4:3), sometimes 352 x 240 (4:3'ish) (VCDs, TV) Afterwards we moved to DVD, which was 720 x 480 (3:2). From there, we moved to 720p broadcast, 1080p broadcast, and 1080p video (BluRay). 720p is 1280 x 720 (16:9) - > 1980 x 1080 is 50% more lines of resolution. Seemed like a logical step. 360p is 640 x 360 (16:9) is 50% less lines of resolution than 720p.  The current standards you'd see in streaming media have more to do with 720p then 1080p becoming overall standards than any mass "circular" theory.

So it's technically correct to only use the term venomous (unless there's a contact poison bearing snake I'm unaware of) but the distinction isn't kept by most people.  So the answer depends on whether you thing grammar should set standards for people to follow or should follow popular usage, which isn't something that anyone has solved in hundreds of years of discussion.

question: When you spray compressed/canned air, what is the liquid that comes out when excessively sprayed?

That's why gas cans get cold when you use them a lot very quickly. Eventually you can release so much gas so quickly, that the temperature drops low enough to stop some of the liquid evaporating as quickly. This is the liquid you see, the same compressed gas that is now so cold, it can't evaporate as quickly as normal.

question: Is this as worrying as it sounds? "Resistance to last-resort antibiotic has now spread across globe"
answer: It's pretty terrible, yes.  R & D on new treatments, especially antibiotics that aren't based on tetracycline, mycins, or macrolides, is slow going and has significant maturation time. In the meanwhile, drugs that are used to treat life-threatening infections will become ineffective. We can still contain this threat, but it will take a concerted worldwide push to totally eliminate unnecessary antibiotic use (such as doctor visits for flu or minor illnesses) and ensure maximum adherence to regimes as prescribed.

question: How does the Stop / start technology in cars work? What is the long term affect of it?
answer: It's pretty simple. When you come to a stop it'll shut of the engine to save fuel. From there it takes you moving your foot off the brake or depressing clutch as the signal to refire the engine and you drive off as usual. It also monitors for things like engine temp and a/c demand to decide if it should start or stop the engine. Because modern engines are so efficient, you start to see fuel savings after only about 6 seconds so it's definitely worth it. These days they're scratching for every tenth of an mpg they can find and in city driving auto start/stop can save you close to 10%. There really are no long term effects that have been noted besides the fuel savings. By the time it'll begin using auto start/stop the oil has warmed up and you don't get cold start engine wear from those starts. Also the starters are much more heavy duty and can tolerate the more frequent use very easily.

question: Why does soda seem to be less carbonated when it's hot compared to when it's cold?
answer: A soda appears to be "more carbonated" when it's cold since the CO2 molecules are more thoroughly dissolved in the soda (the solvent), while when a soda is hot, the CO2 molecules are separate from the soda, making it seem 'less carbonated". Such a difference occurs because gases are more soluble at colder temperatures. This occurs due to the fact that at higher temperatures the gas molecules have a greater average kinetic energy, thus enabling them to break the intermolecular forces which keep them dissolved. Also, at higher temperatures gases have higher vapor pressures which makes them less soluble (this is why manufacturers bottle soda under pressure-to keep the CO2 dissolved). This correlation is evident in the ideas gas law (PV=nRT), since increasing temperature also increases pressure.

question: Autism is a spectrum disorder, which means there are many different types of autism. What connects all of the different types and what makes them all part of the same neurodivergence?
answer: It’s not so much as different types, but different severities. Therefore, the symptoms are all the same but range in prominence. Someone with autism whether mild or severe is diagnosed under the same criterion. This includes problems in the categories of social, speech, and stereotype/fixations (repetitive behavior).  These symptoms derive neurologically. A brain of someone with autism is different than someone without. For example, someone with autism has an increased amount of connections made in the brain. In a normal person, connections that aren’t needed are pruned away throughout childhood. This doesn’t occur as easily in someone with autism, giving the increase in sensitivity to stimulation.  In summary, autism is a spectrum that ranges in severity. It is not influenced by parenting styles or the environment. It is a neurological disorder, not a behavioral. Yay awareness month!!

question: Are birds just idiots or do they fly in front of cars for some crazy bird-like adrenaline rush?
answer: Birds process visual information way faster than us. The reason movies are made in 24 frames per second is because that's enough for a human to perceive that as continuous motion rather than as a series of still images. To a bird 24 frames per second is a slideshow, though, it needs 100 frames per second or more to see continuous motion. Being able to process visual information so rapidly allows birds to estimate the speed and position of moving objects much more accurately than we can, which in turn makes them willing to fly in front of cars. To you that seems insanely risky, but the bird can clearly see it has enough time to make it. Think of it this way: The bird processes visual information at least four times faster than you, so to it the car appears to be moving four times slower than it appears to you.

question: Why are Amazons recommendations so incredibly bad?
answer: Their recommendations are actually really excellent if (and only if): 1) you mostly buy books, movies, and music from them, and 2) you buy a fair bit from them. They started out as a book/media seller and I think their algorithms are still heavily optimized towards those markets. I'm routinely astonished at how good their music recommendations are for me, but I've been buying music from them for close to 10 years so they "know me." But the kind of analysis that works well for media (what did people who looked at or bought this book also buy?), doesn't lend itself well to singular purchases like appliances. Amazon does routinely try to sell me accessories for appliances I bought through amazon, but I agree that the "stuff" recommendations aren't as solid as the media recommendations.

question: Why, when baking, does it matter if butter is 'softened' or 'melted' isn't it the same thing either way? What difference does it make?
answer: No, it is not the same thing. The difference is the texture. When you cream soft but unmelted butter with sugar and add eggs the texture of the semi-solid butter helps to trap air bubbles in the batter, which makes your end product lighter. When you use melted butter you lose this property, as the melted butter doesn't have the structural cohesion to hold the air bubbles in suspension.  Butter also contains a fair amount of water; when the structure is destroyed through melting this water is free to combine with flour to develop the gluten and give a chewy consistency to the end product. This, incidentally, is why cakes not containing butter often depend on whipped egg whites and the support of ungreased pan sides to add that structure.

question: How do speaking accents evolve? I noticed how different people in older movies sounded and it's quite interesting.
answer: Accents generally form when groups become socially or geographically isolated and some groups' pronunciations begin to change. Accents can also spread when people try to emulate them (typically poorer people try to emulate the accents of rich people). As for the accent in older movies, that's called the Mid-Atlantic accent and it was created on purpose. A lot of American actors spoke in a Mid-Atlantic (also called Transatlantic) English accent during the early days of movies. The accent was popular with the Northeastern elite and found its way into theater and movies as a result. It's basically a mix of British and American accents without favoring too much of either. Its popularity declined sharply after WWII. The only American accent I associate with being nasally is the Midwestern accent. I don't fully know the history of it, but I think it's been around for a while though it's not often used by lead actors.

question: Why does my phone screen not respond to pressing when my finger is wet?
answer: Phone touch screens work (well modern ones) based on capacitance. That is a build up of charge between two conductive materials with an insulator in between. So when you touch the glass with anything conductive (your finger and water included) a small amount of charge builds up on the object you touched it with and on a conductor on the other side of the glass where you are touching it. This is how the phone knows when and where you touch it.  When you have wet hands, you inevitably get other parts of the screen other than where you are touching wet. The phone doesn't know what is your finger and what is water. All it knows is it is being touched in multiple places. The results is kind of like you smashing your palm all over it, and you can imagine that doesn't work well.

question: Why is there a broad spectrum of people on juries, and not the defendant's peers?
answer: The statement "jury of ones peers" actually comes from the Magna Carta and not the constitution. The intent was that when someone committed a crime they would be tried by a jury of their social and economic peers, not racial or otherwise. That meant that a noble would be tried by a group of nobles, not commoners, and commoners would be tried be commoners, not nobles since there was a lot of resentment between groups.  Nowadays, the phrase more commonly means that you will be tried by a jury of fellow citizens and has little to do with anything else. Since jury pools are randomly selected from all the citizens withing a given population, and cannot be removed without a good reason (well, technically they can in limited quantities by both sides via a peremptory challenge), they meet the requirements.

question: How nearsightedness and farsightedness work
answer: With nearsightedness, the eyeball is too long for the lens, so that the image often focuses *in front* of the retina.  With farsightedness, the eyeball is too short for the lens, so that the image (if we pretend the retina is transparent) would focus behind the retina.  The result is that people who are nearsighted can still see things close up, while people who are farsighted can see things far away but not close up. Farsightedness, which is uncommon, is often confused with presbyopia, which happens with age and is believed to be caused by the lens in the eye getting less elastic, and thus having less focal range. The symptoms are pretty similar, the inability to focus on near things.

You, of course, get huge bulk discounts by doing this which means that you can make lots of money selling the products individually (if you are a retailer). Sometimes there are no minimum purchase commitments, but this usually means you won't benefit from any major discounts if you only buy one unit. But yeah, that's basically the gist of it. It's a site for suppliers to sell products (usually in bulk) to other companies which typically resell the products to customers, or incorporate the purchased items (e.g. electronic parts) into their own products.

question: How do Rubik's Cube speed records work if the starting cube can have so many different variations?
answer: When you scramble a Rubik's cube, you're never more than 17 or 19 moves away from a solution(I don't remember the exact number, but it's around there). In practice, this isn't how speed cubers work, but the principle is similar. Speed cubers have different processes and memorized patterns of moves to get solve the Rubik's cube. Step one might be get all the edge pieces for one side solved, then solve the corners for that one side, and so on. These moves take about the same amount of time no matter how scrambled the cube is. The only time there is any variance is when solving one step also accidentally solves part of the next step.

question: What's causing the very high pitched engine noise and bangs usually Rally cars produce?
answer: Straight cut gears (used because stronger than the quieter helical cut gears used in most road cars)will whine" at higher road speeds. This makes the loud pops and bangs. Also massively shortens turbo life to around 1000km.

question: Why are humans the only animals with brains as advanced as our own?
answer: Being smart is certainly an evolutionary advantage, but it comes at a cost. For example, for humans to walk on two legs and thus have hands free to use tools etc, and also to have huge brains, it makes human childbirth much more of an ordeal than any other animal, and it also means newborn humans are much more helpless than those of many other species. So it's not that being smart isn't an advantage, it's just not the most economical advantage possible for most species. With tigers, some may be smarter than others, but some also run faster or have bigger teeth, and those traits turned out to be more useful than the bigger brains. The thing about evolution is, it finds *local maxima*. Yes, humans are better adapted than tigers, as evidenced by the fact that we use them for rugs and not vice versa. But that doesn't mean that if you make a tiger slightly more like a human it will be a better tiger.

question: How does a filibuster work?
answer: Filibuster has been part of the Senate rules since the early day of Congress. The majority party could take up the measure again and again in theory, but if the minority filibusters each time, the Senate would accomplish little (or less than what it does now). So if a bill is filibustered, it can either die in that Congress or the leadership can try to amend the bill to make it more palatable to the minority party, or Leadership can file for "cloture" which means that 3/5 of the Senate have to vote in favor of ending debate and move on to a final vote.  & nbsp; The filibuster is a tool meant to protect the rights of the minority. The Founding Fathers went to great lengths to ensure that the "tyranny of the majority" would not trample the minority. By allowing a minority of Senators the opportunity to delay or obstruct legislation they feel would be harmful to their states or the country as a whole, they can stop a majority from trampling on their rights.

question: Why don't we use superglue to mend wounds anymore?
answer: I'm an anesthesiologist, and the surgeons I work with use it all the time. It's not the right closure for some cases. In particular, it's only good for closing skin, not the underlying tissue (so it's useless as a solo item if you have a big laceration). It doesn't stretch well, so you can't use it over joints. It doesn't handle long incisions well, so you don't see it used for C sections. And the medical-grade stuff is expensive.  But if you have a paper cut and want your pain to be over with in a few minutes instead of lingering through next week, it's perfect.

question: What is Emergent Norm Theory?
answer: Emergent norm theory is a way of explaining crowd behaviour and why people in a crowd act collectively. When a crowd forms, people interact with one another and create the social norms for the crowd. People look at each other for social cues - what to do, how to act - and get this idea of mob mentality like 'if everyone is doing it, i'll do it too'.  So for example, a crowd is peacefully protesting labor rights. A couple people in the crowd starts getting rowdy, yelling, cursing, etc. Other people see this behaviour as acceptable and joins in with the shouting. Soon, the whole crowd is rowdy because this is now the norm for them.  It doesn't just have to be violent behaviour, the norms created can be positive depending on the interactions between the individuals.

question: What happened to MySpace and why?
answer: In hindsight, MySpace's initial dominance in the social media space seems to have been a "first mover advantage". They were the first to tap into social media in a way that captured the attention of a critical mass of people. Social media was still a very new world though - an undeveloped market - and what MySpace offered was a niche in the context of what social media has become. Picture present day social media as a big pie, of which MySpace is a little sliver. Most of the pie hadn't been made when Myspace came around, so everyone jumped on board, but as social media has become bigger broader, MySpace basically stayed the same.  Facebook put pictures, messaging and social planning at it's core, and those features appeal to a broader base of people than the MySpace core that includes site ("space") design and music sharing. Subsequently, many of the people that joined MySpace because "OMG, social media" found that newer social media sites (mostly Facebook) actually suited their needs better.

question: Why does sound travel faster in warm temperature?
answer: The reason that sound travels faster in solids isn't actually because the molecules are closer together. It's because solids are *stiff*. A stiff material does not deform very much when it vibrates, which allows the vibration to travel very quickly. A compressible material, on the other hand, wastes energy expanding and compressing with every vibration, slowing down the wave. In fact, a material with a higher density actually results in a slower speed of sound, because it means that more mass has to be accelerated back and forth with every vibration. This means that the speed of sound in gold (~3200m/s) is much lower than in aluminum (~6300m/s), even though they're of comparable stiffness.  So because cold air is denser than warm air, it has a lower speed of sound.

question: If the cleft chin is a dominant trait, why are non-cleft chins so much more common?
answer: Just because a gene is dominant, doesn't mean its feature is going to be common. This is because the frequency of genes being dominant/recessive is not 50/50! Let's say that the non-cleft chin gene is 90% common, and the cleft chin gene is 10%. A simple model would say that this means, roughly 19% of the population have cleft chins and 81% have "normal" chins. These %s only change if evolution starts selecting for one. If by some craziness, suddenly everyone without a cleft chin starts to die, then a few decades later, much more than 90% of people will have cleft chins. But, cleft chins have almost nothing to do with survival - good or bad, and so the proportion of each gene will remain (roughly) constant in the population.

question: What's the big difference between company structure types (Sole Owner, LLC, LTD, Corp)?
answer: The biggest difference is who, among the ownership, is legally responsible for the company's actions. In a sole proprietorship, the owner is 100% responsible. In a partnership, the partners are jointly and severally responsible, which means each can be held 100% responsible (but not to exceed 100%).  A LLC (limited liability company) has two class of owners: manager, who are responsible, and members, who are not. A corporation is owned by shareholders, who, for the most part, have no legal responsibility for the company's actions. The corporation itself would be responsible, and this, in turn, may affect the value of the shareholders' shares of ownership. There are legal maneuvers to "defeat" this protection, and that is called "piercing the corporate veil."

question: What happens in our brains when we don't feel like doing anything?
answer: Let's flip the question: What DOES happen when we DO feel like doing something? It's a pretty broad, complex, and only partly-understood process. One part we have substantial evidence for is the role of dopamine in the mesocorticolimbic pathway in assigning "motivational salience." In other words, while you need many parts of your brain to give a shit about something, there seems to be a sort of targeting system that helps pick out what to give a shit about.  It's not hard to imagine how changes in function there could have serious effects. What if chronic drug use leads to the system focusing overwhelmingly on that substance? What if the system focuses intently on minor background stuff, giving the sense that people are talking about or following you? What if it just conks out and nothing interests you, period?  That said, some amount of apathy/amotivation hits essentially everyone from time to time, in the way that mood and cognition just tend to vary.

question: Why do antidepressants cause suicidal thoughts?
answer: One of my patients described it to me like this: He said that he had always had the suicidal thoughts and could usually push them aside. They were so common and fleeting that ignoring the suicidal thoughts was easy.  Once he started on the medication, the suicidal thoughts were still there, but he could think much more clearly. That meant that the suicidal thoughts were a lot more clear and well defined. Instead of thinking, "I wish I could die," the thoughts become, "I have a nylon rope in the garage and I could punch out a couple tiles in the garage roof to tie the noose." You can make plans and rationalize for possibly the first time in years. That is why suicide happens when people first start taking anti-depressants. Hopefully the person will get a good counselor and discuss the potential effects and be able to offer ways to beat those thoughts.

question: Why/do all the planets in our solar system orbit on the same plane/axis?
answer: Early in the solar system, before the planets formed, the sun basically had "rings" similar to saturn. These "rings" are called a protoplanetary disk. This big disk has to rotate in one direction. If part of it rotated in the opposite direction, it would collide with the other parts of the disk and eventually one direction would win. The planets that form from the gas and dust in this disk are going to orbit in the same direction as the disk. The gas and dust collapse into a single disk for similar reasons. If you had two disks of gas and dust, they would swirl together where they meet, and eventually merge into a single disk. A sufficiently advanced civilization could construct a solar system with planets orbiting on different planes or in different directions, but it would be unlikely to develop naturally. Also, I don't know what kind of orbital instabilities might happen long term if you had things orbiting in weird directions.

answer: I'm going to give you a sheet of paper and a marker pen - you can do what you like, but you're only allowed to touch the paper for a limited amount of time. If I tell you that the amount of time is something like 1/200th of a second, then you're not going to do an awful lot with the marker - you can move it about really fast if you like, but you'll only get a small amount of ink in one spot. If I say to you that you have 10 seconds, you can get more ink on the paper - either in one place if you hold the marker still, or you can make lines by moving it about. It's the same with photography. By opening the camera's shutter for longer, you get more light into the picture. If the light doesn't move, then you get more light in an area that would otherwise have very little - making what could have been a very dark photo brighter. If the light moves, then it'll appear in more than one area of the picture, making a line rather than a point of light.

Theoretically, the force of gravity in the dead center of a celestial body would be zero as you would be pulled the same amount in all directions.  Instead, think of a planet as a collection of atoms, each of which is pulling on all other atoms of the planet. The result is the atoms form into a sphere, as a sphere has the lowest potential energy as atoms move and shift about. Denser elements such as iron will be pulled into the center during this process, eventually resulting in a dense, metallic core.

question: Why do torquey engines make their power at low rpms, but higher horsepower motors seem to hit peak power at higher revs?
answer: If you're talking internal combustion engines, a lot has to do with their bore (cylinder diameter) and stroke (how far up and down the pistons move).   Engines with long strokes typically make higher torque at lower rpms, since to get a long stroke, the throw of the crankshaft is longer. Basically, a longer stroke gives the power stroke more leverage at the crankshaft.  Engines with short strokes can be made to rev faster since the crankshaft throws are shorter. Since the torque at each power stroke is lower since the leverage is lower, these engines need to spin fast to make much power.  Consider the formula for horsepower: HP= torque x RPM/ 5252. It shows how the same HP can be achieved by high torque at low rpm or by lower torque at high rpm.

question: Why are things like cars spray-painted, but others like the interior and exterior of houses are usually painted with brushes?
answer: House exteriors get spray painted too a lot now. But the main reason home interiors aren’t is because of overspray. You have to mask off a lot more stuff if you’re going to spray inside a home to prevent paint from getting on things you don’t want it too. By the time you’re done masking everything you could have brush/roll painted everything already. When cars are painted, they are in a specially ventilated and sealed booth to prevent contamination of the paint from foreign objects like dirt etc.  Additionally, the surface being painted plays a roll. Wood/dry wall hides brush strokes because it absorbs the paint. Metal obviously doesn’t do this so a thin coat is required like what you get from a spray. With a brush the paint would be uneven, drip, and have streaks from dripping down the sides.

This means that if people want to add, remove or change features they can do this and still be backwards compatible with other systems that do not support the same features. This means that a lot of people have added these optional features to the file system over the years which can make it more complex but much more powerful. It also gives the administrators of the machines more flexibility in how they want the file system to be like.
