question: How is the temperature of stars and planets determined (Example: Surface temperature of the Sun is 5,778 K)
answer: When matter heats up (starting from 0 K), it steadily emits some of that heat in the form of electromagnetic radiation. We call this “black body radiation”. This is why, for example, iron turns orange when heated by a blacksmith. As things get hotter, the frequency of these EM waves gets higher. So iron that is “white hot” is emitting higher frequency light than iron which is only “red hot” because the white hot iron is much, much hotter. Most of the things around us are cold enough that their black body radiation is lower frequency than visible light. Our bodies are right around 35 C, for example, and our black body radiation is in the infrared. However, the sun is much, much hotter. By measuring the frequency and intensity of the light emitted by the sun, we can solve for how hot the surface must be in order to produce that color. Our sun is mostly yellow, which works out to roughly 5.7 kK. A blue star is vastly, incredibly a lot hotter, while a red star is much, much colder.

question: What is the difference between genetic and hereditary?
answer: In a lot of contexts, not a lot; a genetic disease and a hereditary disease are practically synonymous. However, hereditary specifically means that something is passed down from a past generation into a new one, while genetic just means having to do with the genes of a being; genes typically get passed down in a hereditary fashion, but they can also mutate independently of the traits of the parents of a given organism; this is the mechanism for evolution. Similarly, hereditary can be used for things outside of genes that can be passed down, like lands or titles (king/queen, duke/dutchess, count/countess, etc) or even heirlooms. While genetics specifically refer to the biological building blocks of the person.

question: In probability, how does the binomial coefficient (n choose k) calculate the possible number of ways you can have k successes in n trials?
answer: So, there are a few factors going on at play here. First, take a look at solely the n!/(n-k)! portion of your formula. This is the total number of possible permutations of choosing k items out of n. So, in this case, given the numbers 1, 2, 3 and I want permutations of length 2, we get (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 1), (2, 3), (3, 1), (3, 2) which is 6 = 3!/1!. Now, we look at the additional /k! on the bottom. In this case, k! is the number of ways to order k items. This serves to eliminate the "duplicate" scenarios, because (1, 2) uses the same elements as (2, 1), for example. So, now, instead of having the total number of \*orderings\*, you have the total number of different ways to choose k elements. The probability bit tacked onto the end of the formula is just the chance of getting one specific ordering of k successes, which when you multiply by the different number of trials you can select gets you the total probability.

question: What happens to debt when a holder of a large amount of debt dies?
answer: Your debts become the responsibility of your estate after you die. Your estate is everything you owned at the time of your death. The process of paying your bills and distributing what’s left is called probate. The executor of your estate, the person responsible for dealing with your will and estate after your death, will use your assets to pay off your debts. This could mean writing checks from a bank account or selling property to get the money. If there isn’t enough to cover your debts, creditors generally are out of luck. This directly affects your ability to leave wealth to your heirs as you have to pay off debts before you can leave money to people. But it also protects them from inheriting some of your debts. Some debts though survive your death and can be passed on to your heirs. Debts like a mortgage for instance. If anyone cosigned debt with you, then they could be on the hook for paying it back.

question: What's the Wall of Sound and how do you use it in songs?
answer: It's technique used (or started) by Phil Spector that created an aesthetic that listeners regarded as having "lots and lots of sound". This is typically a sense of richness and fullness. It combines a few things: 1. consideration for the playback devices of the era. 2. voicing and instrumentation of the music itself. 3. various production effects / recording effects including the use of reverb.  So...you can't "use it" in a strictly recording context - it's not just an effect you apply to music, the composition itself (instrumentation / voices, etc.).  It's best to think of it as an aesthetic - a total production technique - rather than an effect.

However, if you use speech with the intent of causing harm, by inciting a riot, threatening another individual, etc etc, that CAN be prosecuted. But it is not so much the speech that is being prosecuted, but rather what you did with it.  Furthermore, non-government entities can absolutely punish you for your speech, as they are not bound by the first amendment. For example, Facebook banning people who spread the speech.

question: how do e.g. yellow and red make orange
answer: Yellow pigment absorbs mostly blue light, reflecting red and green light. This appears yellow to us, since yellow light itself is between red and green and thus stimulates both color receptors in our eyes a little bit (we can only truly detect red, green, or blue light). Red pigment absorbs mostly blue and green light. When you mix red and yellow pigments, you get something that absorbs lots of blue light, some green light, and no red light. And lots of red and a little green together is what we see when we see orange light (since it is closer to red than it is to green). So that is what we see!

question: What is tetanus and why do they say you get it from rusty metal?
answer: Rusted metal doesn't actually cause tetanus. Tetanus is caused by the bacterium Clostridium tetani, which often resides in soil, dust, feces etc.  Tetanus can be caused by any puncture wound infected with this bacterium. The reason why rusted metal poses a higher risk of infection has to do with the depth of the potential wound (tetanus thrives in low oxygen environments such as deep below the skin) and the fact that old, rusted metal has a higher probability of being exposed to the bacterium. So tl:dr any wound can cause Tetanus, but rusty metal is risky because old, dirty and pokey.

question: What is the purpose of fainting? What are the benefits of this mechanism? In extreme situations (e.g. being under attack) humans and animals sometimes faint but I see this as counterproductive and it would probability be better to become more alert in these situations, right?
answer: Our brains need a *lot* of blood to stay alive. Normally, our bodies work just fine pumping blood against gravity and up to our noggins, but sometimes things go wrong. If for any reason there's a drop in blood pressure or heart rate or reduced level of oxygen to your brain, your brain is going to make you faint. Why? Because it will make you horizontal very quickly, and that will help restore blood flow to your brain since your body is no longer working against gravity. So fainting (technically called syncope) is about preserving bloodflow to the brain, which will prevent brain damage. Preserving your brain is the paramount consideration. If your brain thinks it's not getting enough oxygen, it doesn't care about anything else in that moment. Anything that causes a sudden drop in blood pressure, or heart rate, or blood oxygenation can trigger fainting. Some of these things are physical, and some are psychological.

question: If 1/3 = 0.3333333etc and 2/3 = 0.66666666etc, then how is 3/3 = 1 but not 0.99999999etc?
answer: The explanation is that 0.99999999etc. extending to infinity is the same as 1, so both statements (3/3 = 1 and 3/3 = 0.999999etc.) are true.   While this doesn't seem to make sense initially, there are lots of ways to prove it to be true, mathematically and intuitively.   One of the simplest ways is to say "If 0.99999 etc. and 1 are NOT the same number, there must be a number between them. What is it?" Since it's impossible to find a number between them, they must be the same...  & #x200B; All of the methods rely on (eventually) conceding that infinity is difficult to understand, and/or that the concept of "equals" as shown by the = sign is not quite as simple as saying "these things are identical".

question: Most of not all of us prefer hot showers, due to it being more comfortable. However, same cannot be said said for a hot room to sleep in, which is labelled uncomfortable. Why is this?
answer: Water has a higher heat capacity than air and it also conducts heat better than air. This means that 70 degree air is refreshing for many people, but 70 degree water would have them shivering uncontrollably. The water conducts heat away from the body much faster than air (which is a good insulator) and it also has the ability to absorb and store that heat, making it an ideal material for wicking heat away from the body.  So in order to prevent a shower from sucking out all of your body heat, we use hotter water. When you get out of the shower you also lose heat from the evaporation of the water off of your skin and hair. This is why toweling off doesn't make you cold, but staying wet and letting the air dry you does. So the heat from the shower also helps with the transition when you get out, before you've dried off.

question: what is enriching uranium? How does it work?
answer: Natural uranium that we mine from the ground is mostly composed of uranium 238, with less than 1% uranium 235. Uranium 235 is the useful isotope for nuclear applications like reactors and weapons, and uranium 238 by itself isn't very useful, so we enrich it by increasing the percentage of u-235. This can be anywhere from a few percent u-235 to over 80% u-235 for nuclear weapons. There are several method for enriching uranium, but the most common one is using centrifuges. The natural uranium is turned into a gas called uranium hexafluoride, and then fed into a series of centrifuges. Uranium 238 is slightly heavier than uranium 235, so the u-238 hexafluoride gets pulled more strongly to the outside of the centrifuge and the u-235 tends to stay closer to the middle. It goes through a series of many centrifuges as necessary to achieve the desired level of enrichment.

question: How old was Xenophon during the events of the Anabasis?
answer: It is not exactly known when Xenophon son of Gryllos was born. However, he suggests in the *Anabasis* that he was slightly younger than his friend Proxenos, who was about 30 when he was murdered by the agents of Tissaphernes (2.6.20). It is therefore assumed that Xenophon was not yet 30 at the time of the expedition in 401/0 BC. In his standard work *Xenophon* (1974), J.K. Anderson assumed he was born "a little after 430 BC". In his commentary on the first part of the *Hellenika* (1989), Peter Krentz argued that he must have been born somewhere between 430 and 425 BC. This means he was in his late twenties when he took part in the March of the Ten Thousand. To the Greeks, this meant he was still young - too young to qualify for the office of councillor or general at Athens.

question: What is the earliest recorded hostage situation?
answer: Do you mean the stereotypical hostage-holdout situation, with multiple random people inside and the building surrounded? Or do you mean any hostage-taking at all? Because if it's the latter the answer is probably going to be whatever the oldest war is that we have good records for. Prior to the modern age hostage-taking was politics 101. If you wanted a vassal to be loyal, you took hostages. If you wanted to secure an agreement, you exchanged hostages. The earliest *specific* incident I can point to is the Third Punic War, 149 BC when the Romans demanded 300 noble Carthaginians hostages as terms of peace (they didn't honour it, but that's neither here nor there). You get the feeling from records of the city's reaction that this is an unusually large number, but it's clear that by this time hostage-taking is well-established tradition. I'm also certain that my more learned colleagues can provide many, many earlier instances.

question: The Thirteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution bans slavery "except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted" - what does that part of the 13th Amendment mean?

The prisoners were not compensated in any way, and because they didn't own the workers, and had a steady supply of fresh labor, the overseers had no incentive to ensure the safety of the workers, meaning the working conditions were often even worse than those endured by slaves. Recently freed backs were often unjustly arrested and returned to bandage for crimes like loitering, gambling, or vagrancy, but white prisoners suffered the same terrible conditions.

question: How extensively used/practical was the radio as a method of troop communication in WWI?
answer: > were there practical "man-portable" radios at that time? Nope; most radios were very large sets, transported to the rear areas behind the battlefield and used from stationary positions there. observer aircraft, and eventually tanks, in the British case were used later in the war, say 1917 onwards, to transport wireless sets, but these were not in large enough numbers to make reliance solely on radio feasible.  Power buzzers were used by the British, especially from 1917 onwards, but these could only be used to send messages wirelessly through coded signals (Morse code essentially). They could be intercepted by the enemy, as could most radio signals, so encryption was important (a German *Moritz* listening station picked up a radio message of encouragement from General Rawlinson the night before July 1st, 1916, tipping off nearby German forces as to the imminence of the attack).

question: Why were all early NASA astronauts (those from Mercury, Gemini, and Apollo) from the Military?
answer: NASA's requirements for astronaut groups 1 and 2 included test pilot experience. Group 3 didn't require candidates to be test pilots, but they did require a significant number of flight hours in high performance jet aircraft. Meeting those requirements was essentially impossible for anyone who had not been in the military. Several NASA astronauts were not in the military at the time they were chosen though. Neil Armstrong had been a naval aviator, but he was working as a civilian research pilot for NASA when he was chosen as an astronaut. Elliot See worked as a research pilot for GE after having flown for the Navy.  Groups 4 and 6 (the Apollo-era scientist-astronaut groups) had astronauts who didn't have previous military service. Jack Schmidt (walked on the moon on Apollo 17) is the most famous example. Ed Gibson (science pilot on Skylab 4) also wasn't a veteran.

question: Were "perfume cones" a thing in ancient Egypt?
answer: Yes, its pretty well accepted that the yellow and white cones seen in Egyptian art from the New Kingdom are cones of fat that were meant to perfume the person as they melted. However, they were only worn in scenes where people were meant to be enjoying themselves, like a feast or festival. They were also worn by both men and women in art. Of course, the frequency with which they would have been worn in real life and whether artistic depictions are completely accurate is up for debate, but the basic concept of perfumed cones is sound, as strange as it may seem to us.

question: What are the differences between a princedom and a kingdom?

question: best preserved ancient city ?
answer: I doubt you'll find *any* ancient city where "most of the buildings still stand". What mostly survives are monumental structures, things that people over the intervening centuries valued (for one reason or another) and kept intact. Note that many such structures disappeared as their stone was looted for construction materials.  But all those smaller buildings? Individual houses, shops, tenement blocks, insulae? They're almost all gone. They were built of more perishable materials and no one felt they were really worth preserving. Whereas nowadays we'd love to find more archaeological data to understand how the 'ordinary' person lived, they didn't feel that way in say the 17th CE.  The exception I think is Pompeii and Herculaneum. While the eruption certainly damaged the cities, the falling ash and pumice entombed the whole city and preserved more ordinary houses as well as rich villas.

question: How quickly could Medieval Castles be built?
answer: A basic earth and timber castle could be - and indeed often was - built *very* quickly. William the Conqueror's army threw up a partially prefabricated fort at Pevensey on the very first day after landing. When working with timber and earth, labor, rather than expert craftsmanship or high quality materials, is the primary requirement. There's just not that much to a motte and bailey: it's a ditch, a palisade, and a mound of piled dirt. From all that I've seen, lords in mid-12th century England retained a considerable ability to compel service by their tenants. While I have no specific information on the construction timeline of John Marshal's castle at Newbury - which, incidentally, was not actually at Newbury, but several miles away at Hamstead Marshall - it was a motte-and-bailey castle, and so I doubt it would have taken very long to establish. Weeks, rather than months, would be my guess.

I'm not sure of the origins beyond this but they certainly come from the same root word.

question: What was the mainstream Roman take on the god of the Judeans?
answer: Rome was a hodgepodge of religions, and most people didn't care who you worshipped in private as long as your publicly paid lip service to the official state religion of Jupiter and the like.  Judaism was seen as just another such religion. Many roman soldiers converted to middle eastern religions during wars there and spread them around the empire. But where Judaism ran into problems was that it mingles government and religion. Their king was chosen by god, so pledging loyalty to another leader and religion was tantamount to blasphemy, which led to plenty of political problems for both sides. Hence Jesus' call to render unto caesar what is due or however that passage goes.  This also explains why christianity was pretty much ignored and tolerated when it was still a small religion; it was just another cult. But when it became large enough and its followers refused to publicly worship the traditional roman gods, they clashed with the government.

question: Why didn't Henry VIII disown Elizabeth?

question: Why didn't a Socialist party ever emerge in the US?
answer: During the late 19th and early 20th centuries, there actually were multiple, fairly powerful, socialist parties active in the United States. In two Presidential elections, the SPA received nearly a million votes (1912/1920).  Prior to the formation of the SPA, there were other Socialist parties, including the Workingmen's Party which was formed in 1876 with the goal of "socialist industrial unionism" and was the first Marxist-influenced party in the United States.  Today, there still exist multiple socialist parties, including the Socialist Party USA which claims a membership of around 1,500 and the Democratic Socialist of America which has around 6,000 members.

question: What is the first recorded battle between warring societies?
answer: The first reliably recorded battle was the Battle of Megiddo between Pharaoh Thutmose III and several states in the Levant led by the king of Kadesh. In the 15th century BC these Levant kingdoms had been attempting to switch their allegiance from the Egyptian to the Hittite empire. When Thutmose ascended to the throne he attacked these Levant Kingdoms so as to bring them to heel. The battle was a route and the Egyptians chased their enemy into the city of Megiddo. The city was eventually captured, however, and the king of Kadesh escaped. It would take several years for Thutmose to pacify the Levant, but he would eventually do so, and lead Egypt in her largest territorial conquests.

question: Was South Asian formal wear (such as the sari) influenced at all by Greco-Roman finery?

I think the similarities though are basically due to the simplicity. A sari is basically just a large strip of cloth that is wrapped around the body. When weaving was just coming along, a soft rectangular piece of cloth would be the easiest thing to make and it would just naturally follow that multiple civilizations (including the Greeks and the Indians) would use it as covering. With little need for additional insulation, this style would be functional, simple, and extremely utilitarian and so was quickly adopted and spread.

question: Does a Feynman diagram exist for Wheeler's Delayed Choice Experiment?
answer: Feynman diagrams are not typically used in quantum mechanics, but in quantum field theory. You *can* do it, but there are a couple of caveats: 1. No quantum process is determined by one Feynman diagram. Several of them contribute, the same way that multiple paths contribute to the path integral. You will not find a single "diagram of the situation"; that's not quite what Feynman diagrams are. No one of them tells the full story. 2. There are far easier ways of getting the same results, which is why you're not really going to see this developed anywhere. Splitting the calculation into a large number of Feynman diagrams is a very unnecessarily complex way of describing things. If you want a better understanding I would pick up a book on quantum information theory/quantum computing, where you can actually see step by step how the information gets shuffled around. These are the terms in which a lot of papers on the subject are actually written.

question: How can non-locality avoid violating causality?
answer: The trick is information is never actually transmitted via entanglement. Thus, causality is never broken since you can't actually influence anyone outside your lightcone. In other words, entanglement can only ever produce correlated results, but each result is truly independent and random and you'd never know something profoundly weird occurred until you met with the person with the rest of the entangled system and compared notes. In the classical example of Bob and Alice each with a photon of entangled spin, because simultaneity is not unique, it isn't clear which photon "communicated" with the other as there will be frames of reference where Bob measures his photon first and other frames of reference where Alice measures her photon first. Since no frame is truly preferred, the "communication" has no direction. We just know that each event of measurement is independent and random, but together must be consistent.

question: Why is there no flavour changing neutral current (FCNC) at tree level in the Standard Model?
answer: It's accidental in the SM given the field content---when you write down all allowed terms in the Lagrangian for the quark sector, you can get rid of all but one unitary matrix, the CKM matrix. You can put CKM in the mass matrix so gauge interactions are diagonal (this is the 'flavor basis') or in the gauge interaction so propagators are diagonal ('mass basis'). To rotate into the mass basis, you transform the down-type quarks differently from up-type, so the W bosons (which couple up-type to down-type) no longer couple diagonally. The Z-bosons and photons couple up to up and down to down, so they remain diagonal in the mass basis---hence no FCNC couplings at the level of the Lagrangian. Adding new fields that couple to electroweak will generically give FCNCs unless they look a lot like the Standard Model families. On top of tree-level vanishing, the GIM mechanism suppresses the one-loop effects from W bosons.

question: Do super-capacitors (Electrochemical) work in AC current?
answer: EE major here. AC doesn't mean the current goes from one direction from another, it means that the current (or voltage from v=ir) changes over time. Also, an AC current could mean a dc pulse from some positive value to a negative value. To answer your question, AC current will work. Also, the direction of the current won't "undo" charges. Every capacitor has a positive and negative plate in them, should you reverse the polarity, and run say 5 amps plus in them, they'll just explode. To sum it up, direction of current is not important to a circuit or a circuit element, you can draw current going one way down a branch even if it's going another way, you would just analyze it from there on out with a negative sign. What the circuit and circuit elements DO care about (except resistors of course) is whether or not the polarity is in the correct order i.e. positive to positive, negative to negative and that the circuit is grounded. I hope this answers your question for you, let me know if it doesn't.

question: how does science explain the seemingly mindful and certainly well coordinated actions performed by tiny molecular structures in living cells?
answer: Even though he says it's an accurate representation, remember that you're looking at an animation made by humans for humans. While I don't claim to speak for all of science, I would say this accounts for the "seemingly mindful" behaviour.  An important point about molecular biology is that the single molecules, proteins etc. are moving about stochastically. When a neurotransmitter connects to some binding site, it is not because it was somehow drawn to it, it is because it randomly bounced by, and probably bounced into thousands of other receptors on the way except it didn't fit.  The bit where the genetic replication machinery was working gave the impression that it was sort of floating freely in space. question: Using a large rechargable battery to power a home?
answer: Alright, here's some napkin math: Banks of lead acid batteries are typically used for this purpose. I'm not sure what size is most common (probably whichever is cheapest per watt-hour), but the one in my car is roughly 50 amp-hours, which is ~600 watt-hours at 12 volts. The average american home uses something like 1000 kilowatt-hours per month, or 30 kilowatt-hours per day. 30,000 / 600 = ~50 batteries per day, or ~350 car-sized lead acid batteries to power an average american home for a week. This would take up about 100 cubic feet. A barrel is too small, but you could fill a medium sized shed with batteries and be just fine. Of course, you could also dramatically reduce your energy consumption and get by with far less battery capacity. Use a wood burning stove/furnace, hand wash and dry clothes, use minimal lighting with efficient LEDs, etc. I believe it's fairly common for off-the-grid cabins to have solar charged banks of 10 or so lead acid batteries to power them.

question: How do single called organisms decide what to do?
answer: I strongly recommend Braitenberg's *Vehicles: Experiments in Synthetic Psychology*. It's a series of thought experiments about how complex behaviors can arise from very simple circuits. For more intense reading, you could try *Optima for Animals* by Robert McNeill Alexander. Both authors emphasize that we should be careful to avoid anthropomorphizing non-human entities by ascribing mental states like desires, beliefs, and goals. It's all well and good to talk about those things colloquially as when we say that a thermostat "wants" or "tries" to get the temperature to be at some goal, but when pressed we wouldn't say that a thermostat actually has intentions or desires in the same way that we do. Likewise for all other organisms, whether they be single-celled or very complex, we should be extremely careful in talking about such things.

question: When a small bird defends its nest against a large bird, what threat does it actually pose?
answer: I think you're reasoning that a large bird could obviously beat a small bird, so why bother defending the nest if the large bird knows that? Well if the two bird were to enter into conflict, it would come at a cost to both of them (energy, risk of injury, risk of predation, etc.). Now a bird defending its nest is going to be more likely to risk these costs, because its fitness is tightly linked to offspring survival. A large bird might just be sacrificing dinner. It's an extension of the life-dinner principle.  I'll add that, although size is very important in determining the outcomes of conflicts within species, it's not always a great predictor between species. Sometimes smaller species are better/quicker/meaner than larger species.

question: Could a lot of bees take down an elephant?
answer: The bees don't necessarily have to sting the outer portion of the animal to kill it. question: How are molten salts stored ?

In any case, you'd have to be talking about large amounts of energy to make thermal storage via molten salt worth doing. We're talking temperatures of around 300 degrees C as the "cool" salt and 500+ degrees C for the "hot" salt.

question: Can a low energy pump source applied to a laser gain medium for a long enough duration cause spontaneous emission?
answer: Yes it can, and in high-powered pulsed lasers this is a major problem. With low enough energy from the pump source, you will avoid population inversion simply due to heat dissipation. However, if your pump is sufficiently bright, then you can get what is called prelasing, where there is a laser emission, sourced by spontaneous emission in the laser gain medium. This is usually (always?) lower power than if you were to trigger the system with a laser pulse, but if there are down-stream amplifiers this pulse can still do serious damage to the setup.  Source: worked on a high-power laser system.

question: Why are all techniques of producing electricity based on spinning a magnet in a coil?
answer: There are other ways, very common ways. Some of them you see very day. Batteries use a chemical reaction to pump out electricity, for example. question: How would you test for the location of a gene?
answer: Yeast geneticist here. Do a cross to wild-type and then tetrad dissection. A nuclear gene will segregate 2:2. Mitochondrial genes should mostly transfer 4:0 (cytoplasmic inheritance).  Alternatively, yeast can grow just fine without mitochondrial DNA. You can select for mutants lacking mtDNA and then see if chloramphenicol resistance is also lost. A standard petite selection protocol is to grow cells overnight in a low dose of ethidium bromide, then plate on YPD. Replica plate to YP glycerol and only cells with functioning mitochondria can grow (so the colonies that didn't grow on YPG are the ones you want). Of course, by doing this you'd want to be sure you lost the whole mt genome, and didn't just mess up a few genes on it. There's some basic ways to check for this that I can't quite recall at the moment. Either way, the first method is probably the easiest (do a cross and check segregation pattern).

question: What gives objects their sound?
answer: Objects like to vibrate at some particular frequencies called eigenfrequencies (more or less their "own frequencies" when semi-translated from german to english). When you pluck a string, strike an object, etc, the object will vibrate at these frequencies. These frequencies depend on the mechanical properties of the object (shape, mass, size, material etc.), and can be harmonic (ie multiples of a fundamendal frequency, e.g. for strings), or not (almost everything else). The amplitude of these different components will depend on how you pluck or strike the object. Using a small, rigid thing will give you more high frequencies, striking with a soft object will give you more low frequencies. It also depends on where you strike the object. You can try this with a guitar. Pucking near the end of a string with a pick will give a sharper sound than plucking the middle with your finger. The same frequencies are present in the sound, but not with the same amplitudes.

question: Is asbestos a metal? If so what properties make it so?
answer: Asbestos is not a metal; it's a term for a variety of naturally-occurring minerals (and some synthetic replicas of those minerals) that form long, flexible, fibrous crystals. They're actually silicates - minerals with backbones of silicon and oxygen. They form sheet-like crystals, but small deformations in the crystal structures cause those sheets to curve slightly ("slightly" on the atomic scale, at least); eventually the sheets curve back on themselves and form tubes. question: Are everyones intestines folded up the same way?
answer: Nope! In fact, your small intestine probably isn't even bunched up in the same way it was a month ago!  The small intestine is a very mobile structure because of the mesentery to which it is attached. This means it is able to move over itself and adjust its position (important to isolate infections etc if they occur). Contrast this with the large intestine which is partly retroperitoneal and is fixed as ascending and descending segments. The rest of the large intestine is a bit variable. caecum and sigmoid colon are more mobile, and the transverse colon is a bit mobile but is more specific in its location because its ends are determined by the fixed ascending and descending segments.

question: Is molecular movement really random?
answer: The motion of atoms in many situations can be described classically, in which case it is indeed deterministic. However, it may still be *chaotic*, meaning a small difference in initial conditions will cause a very different result as time goes on, making it impractical to predict the precise paths of a large number of atoms. Quantum mechanics, on the other hand, is generally believed to be truly random. If quantum mechanics is significant in determining the motion of a particle, you can't prescribe one set path it will take. There is no way to predict, for example, the position of an election bound to a nucleus other than as a probability distribution function.

question: Is it possible that all of our scientific theory's could only affect the surroundings we can see? That being earth, our solar system to the farthest we can see in space.

question: What are the properties of a wifi signal?
answer: Wi-Fi works like radio waves, data is encoded into a "carrier" frequency by a transmitter and decoded by the receiving device, much like a cell phone or a radio. The thickness of a wall that a signal can go through greatly depends on the frequency off the carrier signal. The higher the frequency, the faster the connection but easier it is for the signal to be absorbed or deflected away (less penetrating power). The opposite is true, low frequency means higher penetration. High frequency should be for line of sight only. You can change what frequency you want to use in the routers settings. Replacing the default antenna with compatible high gain (ex: 15 dB attenuation) on wireless routers can help alleviate the problems of using a higher frequency. question: When I touch the ends of a battery, why don't I get 'zapped'?
answer: I'm assuming you mean a typical round battery. Let's say you put your thumb on one end and your index finger on the other. The current would have to travel all the way through your thumb, along your hand and then back down your index finger. Your skin simply isn't conductive enough to allow this to happen at the relatively low voltage that is available from the battery (1.5V). But if you take a 9V battery and touch your tongue to it you will get a small zap. This is because the terminals are closer together, the voltage is higher, and the moisture on the surface of your tongue increases conductivity.

question: How was Newton's gravity equation derived if we didn't know the specific quantities involved? How could you check your math with the evidence to verify it's correct? (Such as the masses of planetary objects or the distance between them?) Said another way, how did we compute the masses of planets?
answer: Newton actually didn't know the masses of the objects in the solar systems, because astronomically you can only measure GM, and he didn't know the value of G. Only like a hundred years later did someone manage to measure the gravity between two big lead balls of known mass and determine G from that; this experiment was known as "weighing the Earth" because it allowed people to find out the mass of the Earth. What Newton did was to figure out that in general, an attraction that goes like 1/r^(2) produces elliptical orbits with the Sun at the focus. Since Kepler had already figured out that the orbits are elliptical (using Tycho Brahe's data), this gave Newton confidence that his law was right, even if he didn't know all the numbers.

question: How does the ink of the inkjet printer fall at the right spot on the paper?
answer: The ink droplets are a LOT smaller and move a LOT faster than you think. The droplets are on the order of picolitres, which doesn't mean anything to me either, but just a single one would be very close to invisible once printed on the paper. Consider that printer resolution is on the order of 2000 dpi (dots per inch). Factors like wind and the inertia of horizontal movement simply have no significant effect when you consider the speed the ink droplets are fired out and their incredibly small size. On an inkjet printer, the print head is a column of nozzles around two centimetres in length, so that means it can print a row of an image (or text) which is that height with each pass of the print head. An old fashioned dot matrix printer is actually very similar in this regard, it's just that its pins would be much larger than the nozzles of an inkjet.

question: Why is it that heat energy is so much more "energetic" than other types of energy?
answer: Basically, it's not! It's just that it takes a tremendous amount of energy to heat things up.  Assuming that me and my bike combined weigh 100 kg, the kinetic energy of me riding it at 30 km/h is only: 100 kg * (8.3 m/s)^2 = 6.9 kJ. Enough energy to warm the brakes of your bike a bit if you quickly come to a full stop. Now, to heat a kettle of water, say 1 litre, from 20C to 80C requires: 1kg * 4.2 kJ/kg/K * 60K = 252 kJ. An order of magnitude more energy, which is why we need things like fire or electricity to achieve it. It's beyond the scale of energies that the human body can easily generate.

question: Does tectonic activity contribute to sea level changes?
answer: Tectonic activity can certainly affect sea level. It depends mostly on the speed at which the plates move, which in turn affects the age of the material on the plates. Consider that at a divergent plate boundary, material is being added to the plate. This fresh material is hotter and less dense. Because the plate is then on average less dense, it "floats" higher on the asthenosphere. So, as the rate at which material is added to a plate (which is related to how fast plates are moving apart at a divergent boundary) changes, so does the rate of change of the plate's density. The changes in where the plate "floats" on the asthenosphere affects how much water is displaced. I hope this answers the question. question: Those huge cargo ships and oil tankers have a really small anchor compared to the overall size of the ship. How does such a small anchor manage to keep the ship in place?
answer: The holding power of an anchor is determined by many factors. 1: weight. As ships get bigger, so do their anchors. Most ships anchors are quite large but unless you're right next to the ship itself, the look much smaller. 2: nature of the sea bottom. Sand and mud are great for anchoring a ship; as the flukes really get to dig in as you drop the anchor and pay out chain. Shelly or rocky bottoms are more difficult. 3: scope of chain used and depth of water anchored in. Typically a scope of 5:1 is used when anchoring. Meaning for every shot (90’) of depth use 5 shots of anchor chain. 4: Weather. If it gets windy enough or the current is bad enough; this will lead to a strain on the anchor chain and cause the vessel to “drag” the solution is to either pay out more chain; heave and re-anchor, or get underway until the weather passes. There's a lot more behind the science of the anchor, but I hope this answered most of your questions.

So, red as a far lower refracting angle than blue does, as it has a lower frequency. This frequency dependend refraction is also a problem in lenses for cameras. It is called "color fringing" or "Chromatic aberration", where the lens can not refract all wavelengths to the same point.

question: What colour are subatomic particles?
answer: One would have to consider how color is produced to begin with.  Color is our mind's interpretation of light's wavelength, electrons / other subatomic particles don't radiate light all by themselves.  In fact, you need to accelerate charges (mind you, this is not the only way to create light, but it is the simplest) to create light and make an electron "shine", the wavelegth will depend on how you accelerate it.  Now, if you were to shine light on the electron, this would excite it and it would scatter that light (see Thomson scattering), and again, the wavelength of that light would be dependent on that electron's AND the original light ray's states.  It's sort of like asking what shape would they have, it just really doesn't make sense for subatomic particles to have these properties, color / shape /etcetera is a property of "large", macrospopic bodies composed of many atoms with electrons on them.

question: How come starch does not dissolve in water?
answer: Starch is combination of two types of polymers of glucose, branched and unbranched. Amylose is the unbranched component, and usually has 300 to 3000 glucose units, which wind themselves up into a helical shape held together by hydrogen bonds. This structure doesn't lend itself to being soluble in anything. Amylopectin is more abundant. It's similar to amylose, but instead of a single long helical strand, it consists of helices which branch off into other helices every 24 to 30 glucose subunits. An amylopectin complex usually has 2,000 to 200,000 glucose subunits, and is more soluble than amylose because of the higher number of end points. Starch comes in granules which are usually around 30% amylose and 70% amylopectin, though this varies by species.

question: Why is it possible to control some involuntary bodily functions- like breathing, but not others-like your heartbeat?
answer: Lungs receive nerve impulses from both the autonomic (involuntary) and somatic (voluntary) sections of the nervous system. The heart only receives impulses from the autonomic section. No one really knows why, but a good theory is that it was evolutionarily beneficial to be able to stop your breathing (for if we would dive down to collect seafood). People who could not stop their breathing would drown and die out. People who could stop their breathing while diving for food, or being underwater for any other reason, would survive and continue breeding. It is not evolutionarily beneficial to be able to stop your heartbeat. If it were possible, all people who could (and did) would die. They then would not have been able to reproduce and carry on the unnecessary ability to stop your own heartbeat.

question: How did the glaciers from the last ice age push sediment south?
answer: Glaciers are the most erosive force on Earth. Generally, as they move, they carve the land beneath them. The water where the glacier meets the ground melts into the cracks in the soil and bedrock. As this water freezes and melts it weakens the bedrock’s hold in place. Huge rock pieces can then be captured in the glacier ice itself as it moves (think about when you put a piece of ice on your skin and it sticks for a second, as if it would pick up any loose skin there). In addition, the bottom of the glacier and the rocks it may have captured scrape the surface of the Earth as it travels, causing even more erosion. As the glaciers in the last ice age melted, and the ice started to retreat toward the poles, all of the sediment that was in the ice and under the ice began to be washed away by the melting and flowing water.

question: Why inverse square laws?
answer: Ultimately they all come from conservation laws acting in three dimensions. They all tend to consist of a charge giving off some flux. Electric charge gives off electric flux, mass gives off gravity, e.t.c. If the amount of charge is constant, then the amount of flux coming off it is also constant. If I surround a charge with a sphere, and measure the total flux through the sphere's surface, it will always be the same no matter the size of the sphere, due to the laws relating flux and charge. But as I increase the radius of the sphere, its surface area will increase proportional to r^2 . Therefore, so that the total amount of flux stays the same, the flux density will be proportional to 1/r^2 .

question: What are the deternining factors for how much scar tissue a wound will grow?
answer: The type of tissue (histology), the location, the extent of the damage and the relative health of the patient. Probably the most concise example is the liver. Cihrrosis of the liver is broadly speaking, an excess of scar tissue that has formed in portions of the liver that have been damaged, losing functionality in the process. The hepatic cells (not individual cells, I mean the cluster tissue) are highyl adaptable but do not carry any direct restorative capabilities. Liver damage restored by scar tissue is a very serious problem due to being cumulative coupled with hepatic tissue being unable to restore itself. I.e. constant 'scar tissue' formation. Conversely, the human gingiva has a tremendous regenerative capability both in speed and restoration. A dentist or oral surgeon can make huge incisions or remodeling of the gingiva and have a fully restored gingiva in a very short time without 'scar tissue' coming into play almost ever. I.e. almost never forms 'scar tissue' proper. Etc.

question: Would it be possible to change somebody's blood type by draining their body completely of blood, and then replacing it with a different blood type?
answer: No. In short, blood is created in the bone marrow, and if you just replaced someone's blood, eventually it would die out (erythrocytes live only around 120 days on average) and be replaced by the original blood. However the immune system of the recipient will act much faster and destroy the donated blood much faster, most likely killing the recipient. The only way to change the blood type is to destroy the bone marrow *along with the immune system* using drugs or radiation, and then replace the bone marrow (bone marrow transplant). Of course this is highly dangerous, the body could still mount an attack on the donated marrow or vice versa (graft-versus-host disease) which is something you don't want to have.

question: How do we recognize that something is loud and far away, rather than close and quiet?
answer: I'd suggest that our ears are very good at allowing for a time delay while the sound bounces around in the nooks and crannies of our outer ear. A sound from very far away is largely polarized in such that it is perceived very directly, with waves either entering the ear or being bounced away. Whereas a close sound is far more able to spend a bit of time bouncing around the ears, such that the brain has time to collect both the direct and the bounced data, compare the two and work out that it is likely that the sound is close by. This is an enormous testament to the brains ability to do things so quickly that we literally cannot perceive its action. Its nearly immediately translated into information on the location of a sound.

question: Why does rice suck the moisture out of things?
answer: Rice (like a lot of other grains) is hygroscopic, which means it can trap water molecules inside of it thanks to long biopolymers like cellulose. Rice can gain and lose water in a sort of osmotic balance with the atmosphere. It balances out so that the vapor pressure of water inside the rice grain is equal to that of the atmosphere outside. If you put a wet phone in a closed bag with dry rice, the equilibrium eventually shifts from wet phone and dry rice to less wet phone and wetter rice. Cooked rice is already supersaturated with water, so that's why you only use dry rice to desiccate your phone.

question: How does the emergence of intelligent life and organic matter fit with laws of entropy when they appear to be contradictory?
answer: The laws of entropy apply to a closed system. What you are asking is also basically, "how does a refrigerator separate cold from warm air if that violates entropy? How does one create a more organized system spontaneously?" And the answer is that you don't do it spontaneously. Running a fridge requires a frequent energy input; it turns out that if you put energy into a system, that energy is able to cause a decrease in the entropy of that system. The cost is that entropy elsewhere, like in a heat sink for the system, or in the object generating the energy, must increase to overcompensate. question: How does the Sahara Desert end?
answer: One of the main reasons why deserts exist is because of the global air circulation, which can either being warm rising air which is saturated with water causing rain, or dense, dry air which descends bringing no rain but absorbing moisture. The Sahara Desert occurs around 30 degrees North of the Equator due to sinking dry air of the Hadley Cell, which not only brings little rain, but also absorbs the surface water. The desert ends as you go further South because the warm air travels along the earth's surface absorbing moisture, then rising around the equator, cooling condensing causing rain. As you travel northward the Sahara reaches the Mediterranean Ocean (water) and the Ferrel cell which is the zone of mixing which over laps the Hadley cell, but still has the characterised sinking of cool dry air and the rising of warm saturated air. question: Could a plant chimera only be something like a "grapple," or could there be a tree which produces both grapes and apples?
answer: It is quite common, as long as the plants are of compatible varieties and are closely enough related. Grafting plants together, especially root-stocks to shoot-stocks is a very common practice. Generally it is restricted to closely related plants in the same botanical families, and generally, within there, only amongst closely related genuses.  Certain varieties of apple, pears, and quince may be mutually intercompatible by grafting. I have heard of pear-quince grafting, but I am not sure how apple fits in. They are all in closely related genuses in the family Rosaceae. A surprising one that works really well is potato-tomato grafting. Potatoes and tomatoes are closely related to each other and will graft successfully, producing rather poor tomatoes and rather poor potatoes, but it is interesting. And as a fun fact, tobacco and tomato are both in the Nightshade family (Solanaceae) and are compatible by grafting. So "Tomacco" is actually a completely plausible botanically.

question: If I suspended two large masses in space sufficiently far apart such that they were not moving relative to one another, could I tether them and use the expansion of space between the objects to generate energy?
answer: Yes, there would be a tension in the rope. If the rope is approximated as a spring with spring constant *k* and the current distance between the two rope-tethered galaxies is χ, then the tension in the rope is just F(t) = kχa(t). The number a(t) is the so-called scale factor which describes how proper distances increase over time. The potential energy of the rope due its displacement from equilibrium is simply due to the expansion of space, not necessarily dark energy. (This tension would be there even with zero cosmological constant.) Yes, this energy can be extracted to do work. There is a bit of a caveat here though. This tension would not be uniform throughout the rope. Any signals within the rope travel at the speed of sound, so the central part of the rope doesn't really "know" it's being stretched until the sound wave has propagated from the ends of the rope and reached the center. In reality, the rope will break closer to the ends long before the central part of the rope ever begins to stretch.

question: What is spin in Quantum Mechanics? What function does it serve in QM?
answer: It's just an intrinsic form of angular momentum.  I know that may not seem like a very satisfying answer, but spin is just some fundamental quality that's tacked onto particles - mass, electric charge, spin - they're all just numbers that describes how the particle will behave (though spin is slightly more complicated than charge or mass).  It's an incredibly important piece of quantum mechanics - charged particles with spin have an intrinsic magnetic dipole moment, sort of like a tiny bar magnet. Additionally, spin-statistics governs how systems with multiple particles interact. For example, half-integer spin particles can only be in the same state if they have opposite spins, which is the origin of the Pauli Exclusion Principle for fermions. Bosons, on the other hand, don't give a fuck, and you can pile a bunch of them into the same state - this is the principle behind Bose Einstein condensates, and why you don't have to worry about light bumping into other light.

question: How did language capability evolve such as there are many different languages instead of one universal human language?
answer: Simple answer is that there's no inherent relationship between sounds and the concepts we use to refer to them. Like genes, languages gradually change over time, and any groups that don't speak to each other frequently change in different ways until they're no longer mutually intelligible. In a sense, every language now could be considered a descendant of the language(s) of the humans at the most recent global population bottleneck.  Incidentally, the same thing is true for other animals with language. Whales, monkeys, birds, etc, have local and regionally different languages taught from adults to children. For all relevant species including humans, the particular languages emerged over deep time in parallel with the genes for language (including sound making, hearing, and cognition). If that process took place in disparate environments, each language would be unique, united only by the similar biological constraints on what kind of sounds can be made and grammars can be understood.

question: What happens to the donors genetic code after a blood transfusion?
answer: Erythrocytes don't have DNA! They need all the space they can get for hemoglobin, so right before it is fully mature it packages up its nucleus (where the majority of the DNA is), and ejects it. This package also contains the organelles, including the mitochondria which also have their own DNA.  The good thing about not having DNA or organelles is that erythrocytes don't use any oxygen, they create their ATP via glycolysis of glucose which then leads to fermentation of lactic acid. This means more oxygen for the tissues in your body. Now, there will be some white blood cells in a transfusion, but very few as blood transfusions are almost never whole blood transfusions anymore. When processing donated blood, different parts of your blood are separated out. A 'blood transfusion' is pretty much almost all red blood cells. Red blood cells are filtered to reduce the amount of white blood cells to an insignificant amount. They won't live long enough to have much of an impact on the recipient in nearly all cases.

question: Have two species ever evolved into one?
answer: If what you mean is something like: "bats and birds both evolved wings. Could they resemble each other more and more over time until their genetics are nearly identical, and thus they could interbreed?" The answer is no, and the reason is statistics. Genomes for those species consist of billions of base pairs, with genes in different arrangements. In theory there is a path of mutation that would allow them to converge, but this is akin to the "there's a chance you could walk through a wall" factoid of popular quantum mechanics explanations. Yes, mathematically there is a path where this would occur. No, it will never, ever happen--the chances are so low that it will never happen in a billion universe lifetimes.

question: Why isn't the entire car body used as a radio antenna?
answer: The antenna needs to be resonant at the same frequency you are trying to receive.  For example, if you are trying to tune into a station broadcasting at 100mhz, you know the frequency of the signal, but the radio waves also have a length which is dependent on this frequency. In the case of 100mhz, your wavelength would be about 3 meters. Because of the wave nature, you can have an antenna that is efficient at 1/2 or 1/4 of that wavelength. When the radio waves hit the antenna, it becomes an electrical current that the radio receiver detects and then demodulates.  You can certainly use an antenna that is not resonant, but it will either not pick up enough of the frequency you are trying to receive, or will pick up too much noise from other sources as well.

question: Why is it when I drink something really sour my cheek muscles tighten?
answer: Bit of anatomy and physiology here. The duct of your salivary gland pierces Buccinator, a cheek muscle and is in close relationship with one of the chewing muscles called Masseter.   The sour substance reflexively stimulates your salivary gland to salivate which stretches your salivary duct, irritating your Masseter muscle to spasm. The sour face is actually your Buccinator contracting. The deep pain in the cheek you feel is Masseter spasm. If this is seen in pathological condition it is called trismus as seen in tetanus.  You can actually test this, first clench your teeth, you will feel Masseter just in front of your ear, and if you roll your fingers to the front side of the muscle, you can actually feel the duct. You can feel the muscle contact when you lick sour objects.     You can test your Buccinator by blowing up your cheek. It's one of the important muscle tested for facial nerve palsy.

question: What happens in wooden barrels that gives alcoholic liquids flavor and color?
answer: In the case of bourbon, the oak barrels have been charred before being filled. As the liquor spends years in the barrels, it soaks into the wood, and expands and contracts with the changing temperatures of the seasons. This motion in and out of the burned wood does two things, first, a certain percentage of the alcohol is lost to evaporation through the wood. (This has the interesting side effect of promotion of an unusual species of mold on buildings around aging houses, that feeds on alcohol vapor) Secondly, the compounds originally present in the wood, and those produced in the charring process diffuse into the liquor.  Edit, however, to a bourbon drinker, it's magic, and that's all there is to it.

question: Why is frost more likely to accumulate on my front and rear car windshields than on my side (door) windows?
answer: Net heat radiation exchange is a factor that plays into this. The surrounding environment (trees, houses, hills, and even the ground) all emit heat radiation as a function of their temperature. The more perpendicular a surface is to the incoming radiation flux, the more of that radiation it will absorb (think about it like you are looking at a computer monitor...when you are directly facing looking straight perpendicular to the screen you receive the most light radiation...as you circle around the monitor, less and less of the screen is visible -disregarding LCD view angles - and at 90 degrees you will no longer see any light directly from the screen). The night sky has very little incoming radiation flux, as compared to the ground and surrounding environment. Since the typical front and rear windows are angled up towards the sky, they receive a smaller fractional amount of incoming heat radiation than those surfaces that more directly face the warmer surroundings/environment.

question: Why does listening to my headset mic, which carries a slight delay, make it so difficult to speak?
answer: Part of the reason is that your motor system, which controls all your muscles, relies a lot on the feedback it gets from your senses to control your movements. For example, imagine trying to push a door in a place you are not familiar with. Before you do the movement, you don't know the weight of the door so you will have to dynamicaly adjust your movement to account for that unknown parameter. Regarding speech production, part of the feedback you get is from your ears telling you how you sound. You have learned all your life what your voice sounds like, but, when you listen to it through your headphones, you get a completely different feedback because of the extra delay. This could cause your motor system to think it has commited an error and then try to correct it, explaining why you have problems to produce normal-sounding speech. Like Tokuro said, it could also be that your brain interprets this a new voice which distracts you, but I think my first explaination fits your description better.

question: Why do Black Holes Even Have a Temperature? Why Don’t Black Holes Have a Temperature of Absolute Zero?

Black holes have energy and they have entropy that depends on the energy, therefore they have a temperature. For the properties of a black hole it doesn't matter what is inside. Singularity or not - all that matters is what is outside, because things inside cannot escape anyway.  > How does the black hole absorb this matter and become bigger? This has nothing to do with the temperature of a black hole.

question: While hallucinating, is the brain rendering extremely accurate parts of reality on its own?
answer: The simple fact is we have no idea. However, it seems far more likely that the neural mechanisms of hallucinations should be thought of as a perturbation of normal processes. The theories that usually get thrown around are abnormal spread of neural activity (i.e. activity that codes for one thing "leaks" into other areas) and deficient gating of sensory input (your brain normally selects what data streams proceed into higher areas, this process may begin to fail). But honestly, there is very very little research in this area, because of a) the difficulty in giving hallucinogens to humans and more importantly b) funders don't want to fund it, as in, why fund that when you could fund disease research?

question: Why is it when you close your eyes in a dark room, you can still see colours moving or swirling around?

If you would injest a 5-HT2A agonist like psylocybin, you might see the even more complex interactions of the higher visual complexes, which manifest as alterations in spatial perception and very elaborate geometric patterns.

question: If the boiling point of water is 100°C, why is gaseous water present in the air at room temperature (~26°C)?
answer: The boiling point of a liquid at a particular pressure is the temperature at which the vapor pressure equals that pressure. So the vapor pressure of water is 1atm at 100 degrees Celsius. That means the liquid will evaporate until there's 1 atm partial pressure of steam which is pretty much never going to happen in an open space. At around room temperature, the vapor pressure is around 0.03atm, meaning water will evaporate until the partial pressure of water in the air is 3% of normal air pressure. Now, at room temperature it's also cooler so there's less extra heat around for evaporation to occur so it will tend to occur more slowly. But it still happens.

question: Why does wax burn when it is passed through a wick but doesn't burn when lit on its own?
answer: Before something can be burnt, it must first be vaporized into an acceptable fuel/air mixture. A wick provides a small, localized point where the temperature is high enough for candle wax to be vaporized and mix with air. A solid clump of wax _can_ be lit, but the entire thing must be heated to a temperature where the vapour concentration is high enough for combustion to occur. An analogy would be burning kindling versus an entire log - one is much easier to heat up and ignite than the other, but the latter can still be set on fire when heated enough.

question: If a much larger planet collided with Earth, would we be sucked into its gravitational pull before it actually hit?
answer: Depends on the density of the larger planet. If it were a low density, Hydrogen/Helium planet like Jupiter, the Earth would crash into it before things fell off the surface of the Earth. If the planet had a higher density than the Earth (some kind of Super-Mercury), then once the Earth crossed the Roche limit, the tidal shear of it's gravity would be sufficient that objects of the Earth's surface would fall faster than the Earth as a whole, and would leave the Earth's surface, and impact the other body. You'd die from impact the other planet before the Earth caught up. The Earth isn't a particularly solid body in context (it's made of broken rocks, and a lot of interior liquid/easily deformable bits, so it probably wouldn't just be surface bits that fell off - the upper layers would break into small pieces and also fall apart faster.

As more measurements come in, we can re-calculate the trajectory and our estimate of the collision probability.

question: Why does a blue LED light show up brighter in my peripheral vision than staring directly at it?
answer: Your retina contains two types of photocell; rods and cones. Cones are concentrated strongly at the centre of your vision and are responsible for detailed and colour vision. Rods are concentrated at the periphery of the retina and cannot sense colour or fine detail, but are much, much more sensitive to light. They're responsible for night vision. So, in darkness, where your cones cannot function, your rods dominate your vision and so the periphery becomes more valuable than the centre. Try looking at a faint star with your central vision, then again with the edge. Wiki search dark adapted vision for more info.

question: How did viruses evolve?
answer: They probably co-evolved with proto-cells. question: Does water aeration affect beverage flavor, and if so, how?
answer: I believe the gas that actually affects the taste most is carbon dioxide, though it is typically stated to be oxygen. The carbon dioxide, when dissolved in water, forms carbonic acid, which has a characteristic sharp taste. It is dissolved carbon dioxide/carbonic acid, for example, which is responsible for the taste of unflavored seltzer water. Obviously, there is much less dissolved carbon dioxide in water than carbonated beverages. However, prolonged boiling will drive out the carbon dioxide, reducing the pleasant sharp taste and making the water and resulting brewed beverage taste flat. The pH increase caused by the reduced carbonic acid levels could also affect the extraction of compounds from the coffee/tea, although this effect is much more complicated.

question: Does big flying objects like asteroids when passing through bigger celestial bodies like Earth or Moon alter their gravitational path?
answer: The volume of the Earth is about 1 trillion cubic kilometers. The volume of 1 Ceres, the largest asteroid that we know of is 421 million km. So Ceres is roughly .000421 Earth volume. But Earth is actually quite a lot denser than an asteroid like Ceres, so the actual mass ratio (which is what determines an object's gravitational pull) is more like 0.00015. So to put that in perspective, 0.00015 of 150 lbs is .36 oz, or roughly the weight of one US quarter and a nickel. In summary, yes, there is a gravitational effect, but it's equivalent to the effect on a grown man if someone throws $0.30 past him- that is to say, not anything measurable. And that's assuming that the asteroid passes very close. Gravity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between two objects, which means that the effect at hundreds of thousands of miles is very slight indeed, even for massive objects like the moon.

question: Why are some leaves edible (Like Lettuce, Cabbage and Vines) and others aren't (Like Grass, Apple-tree Leaves, and Oak Leaves)?
answer: Most plant cells have walls made up of the polysaccharide, cellulose. For most herbivores digesting cellulose into sugar is no problem, but for omnivores like humans it's pretty much impossible. Humans don't have the right enzymes, so to us it's just fiber. For plants rich in cellulose we'll end up spending more energy trying to digest the plant matter than we even get out of it. Thus it's futile for us to eat grass or most leaves. Plant leaves that we do eat, like lettuce and cabbage, are low in cellulose and much higher in nutrients. Most have also been cultivated for centuries to be this way.

question: How do bug sprays/powders kill insects just by having it land on them or them stepping on it?
answer: Generally speaking, it depends on what kind of insecticide (bug poison) is being used. The insecticide can either remain on the surface and have an insect step in it (or you have superb timing and directly spray the insects), or it can be absorbed by a plant, and when the insects eat the plant, they get a dose of the chemical. The latter type can be very useful for those pests which attack in a way where one can't efficiently apply a direct spray. Some do both, although I don't know which ones in particular are marketed that way. But basically the majority of insecticides - of either application method - are chemicals that interfere with nerve function (typically either ion channel function or acetylcholine metabolism). The commercially available bug spray Raid (at least the original formula, as memory serves) is essentially a synthetic version of a naturally occurring botanical insecticide. Hope this was helpful!

question: Do balloons filled with helium fly up inside of the iss?
answer: On earth, helium balloons go up not because of anything specific about helium, but rather just because the balloon is less dense than the air around it, and so that air falls down, the balloon is pushed up. This concept is the same reason why some things will float in water and others will sink. If something is less dense than water, it'll rise up in water, if it's more dense it'll sink. The important thing, though, is all of this requires gravity. Without gravity, there's nothing to cause things heavier than air to fall down through it, and nothing to cause things lighter than air to rise up through it. In fact, there's not even a terribly good way to define what up or down is. So just as the astronauts will float in the air without falling 'down', a helium balloon will float in the air without rising 'up'.

question: Why is drinking milk after spicy foods better than drinking water?
answer: Nonpolar substances tend to dissolve other nonpolar substances, and polar substances tend to dissolve other polar substances. "Like dissolves like." Hydrocarbons such as capsaicin tend to be nonpolar, i.e., positive and negative charges are more evenly distributed and cancel each other out. Water molecules, on the other hand, have polar regions, i.e., they have partial positive and partial negative charges. The arrangement and orientation of the atoms within a molecule help determine its polarity. Since water is polar and capsaicin is nonpolar, capsaicin is less soluble in water than it would be in a nonpolar solvent. The capsaicin would still be free to interact with receptors that cause pain. Milk and other dairy products contain casein, a nonpolar protein that is better at attracting the nonpolar capsaicin than the polar water molecules. If capsaicin is interacting with casein instead of the receptors that cause pain, then the burning sensation is lessened/neutralized.

question: Why does melanin make skin darker?
answer: It doesn't have anything to do with heat. As I understand it, melanin is produced in response to ultraviolet radiation. More UV will lead to more melanin being produced. That's why you tan. Melanin will block UV from reaching the delicate underlayers of your skin, because too much UV is bad for you. However, UV in some amount is necessary for your body to produce vitamin D in your skin. Too little vitamin D can cause rickets and other diseases. So if your ancestors came from an area with high levels of UV, such as areas around the equator, they will tend to have higher levels of melanin so as to block more of the UV. If your ancestors came from higher (northern or southern) latitudes, there isn't as much UV, so you won't need to block as much, and will need to absorb more of it. So you make less melanin.

question: The Earth really is flat. And you're part of an exploration team to discover what lies beyond the edge.
answer:
" Get up and go, gentlemen. The last one of you up goes over the edge without a rope."
They called us explorers, told us that we were the real scientists who were pushing the boundaries of what we knew of our earth. But the GPS trackers and armed guards surrounding us reminded us of our past. We were debtors, given the choice to die in a quick fall off the face of the earth, or rot in prison repaying our debts with years wasting away.
I hooked myself in to the ground plate, and walked over to the last rock jutting out over the dark abyss. It felt like a walk along the plank to step lightly across the stone. I turned around, and crouched down at the very edge. To my left, I saw four or five others getting into a similar position. I breathed in deeply, and then pushed myself backwards. I had no intention of investigating what lay below the surface, only to end my life in a quick manner. The rope betrayed me, though, and caught on the safety release. I was left hanging in darkness, spinning around endlessly in the abyss. I managed to pull a knife from my belt, and began to saw through the rope. It was slow going, but my frantic pace made quick work of the knotted string that held me away from the inevitable end.
Then I fell. Simply fell. Never to rise again.

question: The gatekeeper between hell and heaven sees many applications daily to transfer from the former into the latter. Today, for the first time, he saw someone wanting to go the other way.
answer:
" So let me get this straight. You, someone who was chosen to go to Heaven, want to go to Hell?"
" Yep."
Still puzzled, the gatekeeper asks, " Why?"
The man smirks and simply says, " To Hell and back."
The gatekeeper looks at the man confused, examining him as if he could see a reason why he wanted to go to Hell.
" Elaborate," said the gatekeeper.
The smirk on the man's face changed tones from one of cockiness to despondency. His fist tightened. Looking down, the man repeated solemnly this time, " To Hell and back."
The gatekeeper felt the change in his attitude. He noticed what appeared to be a photo in the man's clenched hand. He sighed, " You're a damned fool, you know that?"
With that, the gates opened.
The man looked at the gatekeeper and said, " Thank you."
The gatekeeper smirked and said, " To Hell and back."

answer:
It's 29 March 2015, Sydney. Final match of World cup 2015 is on its way. The defending champions India are playing against first timer Germans in this epic battle of world dominance.
Germany's impossible path to finals has been a truly exciting journey. The team which was not even qualified for world cup got last minute invitation, due to sudden withdrawal of Afghanistan. and Germany with its imported players from India set out to prove themselves under the captaincy of Asif Khan. They had bested Bangladesh, Scotland, New Zeeland and England to reach qualifiers. They had trashed Pakistan to get to semi-finals, and won by just 2 runs against Shri Lanka to get to the finals.
And here they are just six runs way from victory with one ball remaining and eight wickets down. They are facing mighty Indians. This is unbelievable moment for fans all over the world. Pakistan had found themselves at similar situation all those world cups ago, and WON. Now the question remains, can they do it? can Germans hit the finals boundary for maximum runs and win the world cup.
Indian medium pacer, Bhuwaneshwar kumar taking his run up. All the mighty batsman have bowed before kumar before. odds are highly stacked against German batsman Shafraz Samsudeen. Shafraz the only real german in the team has no previous experience of batting internationally. The presure is ginormous. Kumar bowls full toss, Shafraz swings the bat blindly and....
Well you see, *world cup* may mean different thing for different people. since I had no interest in football (some guys call it saucer?) I thought I would write on cricket World cup.
P.S.: The player names are all real.

question: " Incoming! Dropships, coming in over the bridge! "
answer:
Streaks of red and green smoke followed the ships.
" Merry Christmas everyone!" cried the President. Wrapped gifts drifted down on parachutes, descending at the same speed as the snow. Strangers hugged, lovers kissed, a few phones filmed the festivities. The President laughed and smiled over the hum of the ships. When the dropships hovered at eye level, the bay doors fell down.
A couple dozen drones disguised as elves poured out. They ran, leaped, and danced through the crowds, handing out sweets to every out-stretched hand. One elf soared next to my window, tapping on the glass and waving. I waved back. The hot chocolate in my mug kept my hands warm and I found myself smiling. The giant projection of the country's benevolent leader, the street with lights of every colors, the people crammed shoulder to shoulder, happily sharing each others' warmth. It was a picture perfect holiday.
A small girl tugged at the arm of my sweater. " Let me finish this cocoa." I whispered to her. She nodded and skipped to the front room. I drank what was left, putting the mug in the sink. She was already waiting at the door, holding my coat for me. " Let's go."
We walked to the cemetery. Her hand was still warm despite not wearing a glove. We stopped at a gravestone with a picture of a young woman. " Hi Mommy!" the girl said. The dates beneath the picture read December 25th, XXXX - August 31st, XXXX.
" Ready?!" The little girl placed a small cake with a candle in front of the gravestone. " One, two, three..."
" Happy Birthday to you..." The snow had stopped, the clouds cleared up to a half moon.
