question: Write the second half of a story whose first half doesn't exist.
answer:
Sonnet Number Six
And all the troubles ended with a deft
Maneuver of the hero's cutlass blade.
The villains died, their followers all left,
And good again could rest in the peace they'd made.
No funerals for fallen comrades were held
And all their loved ones lived with no hardship.
The pain of loss was felt by none, but welled
The tears of joy for reunited friendship.
War was won valiantly by the victorious.
No sacrifices were made at all by citizens.
Because the worries are what is laborious,
And winners don't fear loss or reticence.
The streets all echoed with a jovial laughter;
All lived as happily as ever after.

question: By 2345 humanity has colonized most of the solar system and have started sending probes beyond sol, when one day, a frantic interstellar message is received saying " do not leave the sol system "
answer:
It took us a thousand years after we first got the message. One thousand years of scientific study and engineering breakthroughs. The first hundred years was us trying to deny the message. We sent out probes, only to have them destroyed as soon as they traveled exactly two light years away from the sun. We tried different types of stealth coatings, holographic cloaks, and other more exotic measures. None worked. As soon as any craft reached the two light year distance limit, they were destroyed.
So we stayed in our home system, colonizing every celestial body that orbited the sun. We even created vast colonies that danced above or below the solar system orbit ring. We examined the surrounding space as best we could. We saw other life-bearing planets nearby. We even saw a brief flash of an alien probe that tried to go farther than their two light year limit.
Something had claimed the space between the stars and was refusing all travel. So we watched and we studied and we learned. We discovered the matter annihilation field that kept everyone contained within their systems. We discovered its weakness.
And so almost one thousand years after we received the edict, we put in place our answer to it.
That was the day when the Sun, the Earth, and all the planets and stations in orbit broke away from their place in the galaxy and started to move together towards the next nearest star.
If we could not leave the sol system, then the sol system was going to come with us.

question: A man dies twice: once when his heart stops beating and once when his name is said for the last time.
answer:
" Who was Abraham Lincoln?" Xan asked, as he leafed through an old US history textbook.
" What does it matter? The fire is dying." Replied Garros
" I don't know... He's this guy, on the cover." Xan lifted up the text. " He just looks... Dignified. Like he did something he was really proud of. Maybe it was something great. Something they were all proud of. Something untouchable."
Garros reached his hand to Xan and gestured to see the book. Xan passed it over. Garros stared at it with exploring eyes. He wiped a mode of dust off the man's solemn face and ran his fingers over the portrait on the books cover.
" Nothing is untouchable." Garros tossed the text into the furnace.
Xan watched as the bearded face became disfigured in the flame. Garros noticed a dejected look in Xan's face and his tone turned sympathetic.
" Hey. Anything that we find here is just the past. We don't need to dwell, it's almost like it never even happened..." The two paused as Xan continued to hypnotically gaze at the flame. Xan briefly shook his head, snapping out of his trance before focusing his attention to his partner.
" I guess you're right Garros... Come on, let's get back to the camp and see how the humans have progressed on the Psaber monument."

question: Her hands had been caked in soot for as long as she could remember, but she didn't mind. In the end, all of the black dust was worth it.
answer:
We burned them.
All of them. All of the decided and damned and dreadful. What a fire they made too, licking the walls of the hall dancing images of God upon all of us unworthy. Elder Septer Kane found them dredging in the blackness of the Old World, hunting and eating the plants that could cling to the soiled earth the old peoples had left behind to dry in the sun. Naked and afraid they listened to the old mans words of a great hall in the distance, filled to the spires with food and books. How they loved books.
Elder Septer Thome says the people in the Old World love books because it distracts them from their poison blood and cracked skin. Tell them you have food and they will be skeptical. They will talk quietly in their old tongues and their new ones too. If you tell them you have books and they will fall at your feet and kiss your legs. They will follow you to the end of the scorch and to the end of forever too.
I never knew anything other than The Burning. It was my duty to stand on the pedestal of God, and fill the pit with tar and oil. The Elders told me I was part of a beautiful machine. A tiny beautiful cog. One day it will be my job to bring in the wanderers with their poison blood, but for now, I just burn them.
I dont even hear their screaming anymore. All I hear is Gods music, he sings about how much he wants to return to us when we purify our home.

question: The monsters that everyone thinks is following them at night? Yeah, only you can see them.
answer:
At first, I thought it was a curse.
But I spoke to them.
Great pits for eyes, long and boney fingers with claws dragging behind them as they walked. Maggots, and roaches crawling under their dry skin stretched taut over the thin frames.
But, it was the first time they'd ever been given attention.
They were without plausible reaction. Grunting, screeching, slamming their arms down - but they never harmed me. Why? I could touch them, I could smell them.
I taught them to speak. Quickly, their language skills degraded, but it was a beautiful pidgin we spoke.
It didn't take long. I was a back-alley God. I ruled the places where the dangerous feared to stalk. They carried me above their heads, cheering for me, " God! God!"
But the others, they couldn't see them. My loyal followers. I read for them. Books about war. Killing. Fighting. I forged a race of warriors almost overnight.
Soon, we will rise. From the depths, muck and sludge, but we will become golden. We will all become King, I will forge a new world order, with my loyal servants all beside my throne.

That's not happening in your mind, you know. And of course the blackness is growing, because everything, *everything* starts from a thought. Just not in your cursed stupid human head.
Even something as simple as the end of the world as we know it.
I can always think up another one.
Sigh.

question: The world's first 100 % successful total head transplant is completed between an individual paralyzed from the waist down and a braindead patient. The only problem is that, contrary to all research up to that point, human consciousness does not reside in the brain.
answer:
The surgeon looked at the two unresponsive bodies.
" Why did you take the time to put the brain dead patients head on the paralyzed body?" said a nurse.
The surgeon ignored her.
" I don't understand. The science was solid" said the surgeon
" I mean he's braindead right? So just, I don't keep the head for science or something"
" He should be up and moving by now"
" It's not like when we do a heart transplant we take the bad heart and put it in a corpse"
" Where did I go wrong?" said the surgeon turning to slam his fist against the wall.
" Probably when you thought to yourself'you know what? I'm going to stitch this brain dead head on to that paralyzed body"
" This was supposed to be my defining moment"
A white light filled the room. The surgeon and the nurse turned to the four foot tall elfin creature in the middle of the room.
" We're really not supposed to do this but you just seem so beaten up about it so, the flinglin"
" What?"
" Human consciousness resides in the flinglin"
" What's the flinglin?" said the surgeon
" Oh are you guys not there yet? Shit. Ok uhm…this was a dream"
The elfin creature disappeared in a flash of white light.
" So now it makes even less sense that you took the time to switch the heads"

question: A man sits in the desert playing a piano.
answer:
The sand blew around Johann as he ascends a set of old dried stairs. A withered bench long since bleached white sits neatly next to an old piano. Johann brushes the sand off and fixes himself down on the familiar wood. His old hands run a cursory dance along the keyboard and the melodious notes break through the hot simmering air. Johann looks up. The sun sits high in the sky, it's there at the same time, every day, the only remaining member of an audience long gone.
It was a slow process, desertification. Sand crept up on the land through storms of wind. Johann's neighbors and their neighbors have all since packed up and moved north. Their colonial New England houses were never created to withstand the constant blasts of heated sand, and they eventually fell, leaving only a skeleton of supports and mementos of a life long gone. But Johann stayed. He stayed because he had made a promise.
Johann starts with her favorite. It always brought a smile to her face, even in the worst of times, and he imagines it no differently today. The sand around him picks up and dances along. He works himself through many classical compositions, Tchaikovsky, Mozart, Beethoven, Bach. He plays them with his heart, because he knows that it may be the last time they're ever played. The wind picks up, and the dance becomes a riot. Tears stream down Johann's face as the storm rages around him.
The next day there is no sign of a house, no sign of a piano, no sign of music. And the man in the desert plays no more.

answer:
I'm running now, running because I'm sick of the lights.
You see, with every day that passes, there are more lights created, more security over the shrinking unknown.
Since the beginning of humanity, we've used light to guide us, light as a symbol for hope and all that is right and noble in the world, and the cruel twist in that is that our very vision is what blinds us.
I believe in touch, mainly. Touch and taste and smell, because these senses are direct. What I feel by touching is what is directly connected to me, mentally as well as physically tangible, grounded, real. How can I trust my sight claiming that there is a lamp post three feet away?
Who's to say that my brain isn't just interpreting the light incorrectly?
Soon, they will send someone to find me, and they will find me using lights. question: The decidedly not-safe-for-children origin story of Santa Claus. How the man in red really got his start
answer:
The weight grows heavy on his shoulders every year around this time. You might hear stories about his brave trip around the world, delivering packages to good children and spreading good cheer. The truth is, there are no good children left.
He stays inside, unable to face the world that shuns him. That fateful night in frigid Siberia remains a day to mourn and a day for blame. Clauz carried a wounded child through 7 miles of tundra to the nearest medical center, absorbing her blood into a sweat suit he would never wash. The guilt of the dead hangs over him like a fresh cut of mistletoe, beckoning him to seek the kiss of death like she did. What cheer could he bring, now? The life of a man plagued by the jingle jangle of the train track, which rang into his ear as he took each step. The rosy-cheeked recluse only comes out at night, and only once does he set foot into town to the home of the little girl he failed to deliver. The last good girl left.
Stepping into the starry night sends memories through his tired hands. His grip is stronger now, able to carry the same crimson-stained sack. His yearly pilgrimage steers him to her home, where he lays 12 wreaths for every year he has mourned. The family greets him with sympathy, and sends him back with a package of milk and unleavened bread.
The morning comes, and Clauz begins his penance.

question: In a Future world, you are one of the postman of death. Your job is to go door to door to inform people 24 hours before their death.
answer:
I glanced over my transponder of death, the list of addresses and names many times longer than it should be. *sigh*. It was going to be one of *those* tomorrows.
This was my career. The grand job AI was never wrong, and I knew in my heart it was what I was born to do. The problem these days was people. They just don't understand the kindliness and community that comes with having a door to door job. Sure, you had your milkman, then the postman, and now with robots it seems we're the only job left that fits the bill. Heck, most people don't even have to leave their apartments these days when then can virtu-commute and have everything else delivered right to their door.
Nobody appreciates a visit. There was never a " Hello there, how can I help you?" but only " Boo hoo I'm dead." Where happened to the good old days where the rowdier types would at least pull a knife and make it interesting? People, they just don't understand.
This was my career, and I need to do something to return it to the glory days it once was. What was a postman without going postal?
*sigh*. It is going to be one of *those* tomorrows.

answer:
Once upon a time there lived a little girl called Moonshine.
They called her Moonshine because her hair glimmered and shone like a sword being swung in the moon light before slicing someone's skull in two.
Moonshine lived with her Mother, Father and bastard Brother in a small holding in the woods.
A bastard is special type of boy who is born because Daddy couldn't keep it in his trousers.
One day, Moonshine was out walking in the woods with her bastard Brother. When all of a sudden a witch appeared from behind a great, big oak tree. Moonshine and her bastard Brother were scared.
'W..w..what do you want?' Asked Moonshine.
'I want cut out your eyes and grind them into a powder that I can give to the Great Water Wizard as an offering. Give me your eyes Child or I'll kill your family'.
Little Moonshine was scared. But she loved her family so so much that she took the hand of the witch and went away with her. Never to be seen again.
And her family lived miserably ever after.

question: After the apocalypse, you are the last surviving piano player in the world. You live in a small town, but no one has tried to learn from you because all spare time is used trying to survive. One day a man walks in and starts playing Mozart.
answer:
It had been so long. I thought I would shuffle from this coil with the regret of bringing dying knowledge with me into oblivion. It was my greatest regret. Despite all the death, it was the most painful thing of the apocalypse. So much beauty, gone with me.
You can not imagine how excited I was when I heard the keyboard playing from across the room. I see a man, a stranger, sitting in front of it with his hands by the keys. Mozart. I would recognize it in a chord and he is playing flawlessly. The body of the board blocks his hands, and I desperately need to see them in action, to see another technique. I've missed watching others play for decades.
I stumble toward the beautiful sound. My old bones ache and I have trouble catching my breath. Its hard to stay healthy without doctors or medicine and I would be old and sick even if the apocalypse had never occured. My heart beats faster than it has in years and it aches in a scary way. I ignore my aches and continue. This may be the last important event of my life.
I come close enough to see his hands over the top.of the keyboard. They sit still on the keys. No movement, no technique.
He pressed the autoplay.

answer:

These powers were never meant to be known outside of his homeland - never. They were not supposed to be revealed to the outsiders who would despise them and end them. They were meant for the betterment of his people; his culture. And the connected world he now lived in, and helped create, would not stand for it. The show was on. Hitler bowed to the audience and removed his gloves, and with his hands gestured towards a cowering family.
" Tonight I shall amaze you. Watch me make this Jewish family, *disappear*!"

question: In a magical world Necromancers make a good (albeit controversial) business by bringing back clients from the dead. Today is your first day as an intern at one such clinic.
answer:
The waiting room looked like one for an expensive medical office with leather couches and ornate wallpaper. Sally, who manned the desk, was typing in a new appointment. I stood akwardly in the doorway with a file.
" Mr Coltnoir?" I called. A middle aged man looked up. His head was shiny and his eyebrows were missing. When he grinned his teeth gleamed.
" That's me." He followed me to Nec. Benson's room.
Benson had graduated in only three years and completed her rotation in six months. She was an inspiration. Her pro bono work was famous as well, mostly focusing on providing services to Amnesty International.
" Are you new?"
" Yes."
" You look a little nervous."
" I'm interning."
" Fun."
He didn't sound local. I took a peek at this chart. Quebec? That was really far. And he had cancer. Stage Four, and sitting on the top of his spine.
That sucked.
He took the chair in front of the desk. I checked his blood pressure, reflexes, and did the medical history. He took it with good humor.
" So, how long does this take?"
" Well," I closed his file. " This is just the consult. We're going to cover options, timeline, payment. All that."
" I've done my own research."
" Is that why you came here?"
" To Mexico? Yeah. Best in the business with the Aztic foundation."
" Well, there First Nation structure in Canada is interesting."
" Do you know a lot about it?"
I shrugged. " I did a paper on the Pacific Coast Coffiners of'86."
" Wow." He fiddled with a brochure. " That's cool."
" You have enough idea what I'm talking about, do you?"
He laughed again. " Nope. But I'll look it up later."

question: You cut your fingers. Instead of blood, ink runs from the wound.
answer:
I had never bled before. I was clumsy, but in a manner that was apparently cute, rather than destructive. Slips and trips were simply part of the daily routine for me, but my character trait had never had any consequences. I never so much as bruised, never mind actually breaking the skin.
I was determined to change that. I swiftly drew the knife across the palm of my hand, marvelling at how easily my skin parted. Almost like the pages of a book. My reactions were muted; there was very little pain. No consequences, after all.
The thin, blue liquid dripping from my palm seemed proof enough for what I had suspected for some time. I wasn ’ t real. I was a poorly written creation, with ink running through my veins and stock tropes in place of a personality.

question: You have only been yelled/screamed at in harsh tones your entire life and now encounter normal, kinder tones. How do you react and feel?
answer:
True story. Having spent a great deal of my childhood in various foster homes while my alcoholic mother kept taking me from my dad's custody, I got used to constant yelling in a cigarette filled alcoholic fueled home.
My dad was rarely cross, and I finally got to be with him full time in High School, but sometimes my kids see my rage in my voice, which I regret every time. I quickly apologize and this has been minimal as I get older, but it's still a struggle. My kids, to their credit, have been great and our relationship sound, thank God. I do not drink or smoke and have provided them a decent middle class upbringing, and have been married to their mom their whole lives > 25 yrs. I hug them every day, even the grown ones, and I always tell them I love them. ALWAYS.
Now, to your question. I am still constantly moved by people who remain calm and speak softly to me when I am upset or there is a tense situation. Frankly, it makes me start to cry, but I hold it back....and for the life of me I can not control this response. I think my nerves are constantly on high alert, because to survive as a child, I had to stay calm and quiet to avoid beatings or being yelled at. I have older siblings, some are dead, but my brother who lived with me during these years protected me by taking most of the beatings. He died 2 years ago, I miss him every day.
I'm a fairly tough guy. 6'4, 280 lbs and looking at me or casually knowing me, you would never know this is what happens when people speak softly to me.

question: When you die in this world you go to the next... and the reverse.
answer:
It took a hell of a lot of planning.
You see, it was one thing to know that dying here sent you back to Earth. It was another to actually achieve it. The whole point of this place is for everything to be perfect and suffused with happiness. Death didn't really fit that program. It's not that there was no way to die, it's just that they didn't stick. You could do whatever it was that made you happy, and that would have no consequences. Jump off a bridge and you'll get the rush of adrenaline, hit the ground and be able to go right back up for round 2.
Our guardians though, they had weapons. Flaming swords. They were meant to defend us against anything. That meant they could kill anything, or anyone. The challenge was getting one. The guardians never slept, never stopped their unending vigilance. You would have to be a better thief than Earth has ever seen.
Luckily, I had eternity to practice.
I got a sword, though I ended up having to kill it's erstwhile bearer, watch it burn and dissolve into nothing. They don't have another world to go to. Not like me. Throw myself on the sword, and here I am. Planet Earth.
Quite a lot has changed since I was last here. There's a lot more people round, for one thing. Good, that should make the next task easier. And the sword came with me? Even better.
I managed to slay enough to balance out a whole lifetime of good deeds before they killed me, and then some. Heaven bores me now, it's high time I gave Hell a spin.

question: Describe peach in the most vivid way possible.
answer:
You see it, soft and glowing, yet delicate and blushing. A light tone that constantly reminds you of peace and calm. It ’ s not as fierce as the sunset over a body of water. It doesn ’ t burn with the strength of a suddenly lit light in a dark room. Nor does its shade ever remind you of a city ’ s night sky. No, it is a pale bright, pleasing to the eyes and as round as a pigment can get.
And just like it ’ s appearance, it becomes soft to the touch. Some say it is like the fuzz on a newborn ’ s cheeks. But it has the roughness of a suede cushion being stroked one way and the other. It has no sharp edges, just the lumps of nature. And although it is round, it is never a perfect sphere: small enough to fit in one palm.

question: A zombie plague has overrun the world, except for two pockets of resistance in Los Angeles, controlled by the Bloods and the Crips.
answer:
" How do you kill that which is already dead?"
That simple question will be etched forever in my mind. We saw it on television, we heard it on the radio, and we felt it in the silence of the streets. Half the world was panicking by the time we'd heard, and I reckon the other half was already limping around with their innards sticking out.
You'd think that the hoods would be chaos, looting, murder, and everything else. That's not chaos, though, that's just the hood. No, it was beverly hills that was turning into a war zone. Something about people who have had it all handed to them on a silver platter, when someone comes to take it away now it's them that are acting like " thugs".
But down here, where most of them wouldn't even drive through in their Mercedes, that's where everything became quiet. That's because we all knew the only thing that mattered, we didn't have our nice cars, big meals, or swimming pools to worry about. Down here all that matters is family.
Which brings us back to the original question, " How do you kill that which is already dead?"
Good question, because everybody around here died a long time ago. Something about seeing your own brother get capped over a sixteenth of an ounce makes it so you can't feel anymore. So when LA was burning to the ground, and everybody was going mad, all we could hear on the news station was " Chaos, Chaos in LA."
Hell, I grew up in chaos. bring it on.

Friends we're not, you dare pretend?
Have we not known each other well?
It's your smug tone that I shall quell.
Smug? Not I, believe me I pray.
Ha! You think it is the end of days?
No dear me, just hear me out!
What is all this you're on about?
It's this charade, I can't partake.
Charade? You fool, the world's at stake!
We have been at it for centuries.
And I will win, one day you'll see.
You see an end to this old fight?
If not then why would I play knight?
Have you not, like I, grown weary?
I dare say, the routine is dreary.
Aha! You see, it's lost its splendor.
But you were, once, a fierce contender.
It's the routine, you see, I no longer care.
What then have we? I ask, I dare.
We can agree, a new game, new rules.
I will not be made your fool!
If you agree, we split the earth.
I take south and you take north.
Aha that's right! We each take half.
And from there comes what, may I ask?
We fight to recruit, to summon souls.
It's dark, I'm intrigued by this goal.
We each shall play, to lure them close.
Well then you shall win, you're so verbose.
We each have tools at our dispense.
They will be helpless, without defense.
This is the game, if you accept?
I'll play this game, become adept.
Then here we are, a new cease fire!
A new triumph, I will aspire.
After time, we will count, take toll.
Then, alas! The victor we shall know.
And from there, eternity.
A new game we'll have, I'm sure, we'll see.

question: You're born with a genetic defect making you bullet proof, but you had no idea until now
answer:
The riot was over, the thick black smoke of a burning car fed up into the night sky and framed perfectly against the faintly shaking orange light. It was rather beautiful, even from my slightly stilted view lying on my side on the cold tarmac. I had been lying here for a while, thinking on my life, my choices, what had lead me to this moment. As it turns out I can get pretty philosophical when I thought I was dying.
The ringing in my ears meant that I couldn't hear the mutterings of the police officer that had shot me. Asking his superior what he should do, if what he did was right, poor guy. It wasn't until then that I realised I felt fine.
I sat up, slowly, sluggishly and looked down at the hole in my shirt, not a drop of blood around the entry and the faint feeling of something warm resting against my belt. I reached under, wrapping my fingers around the object and producing a small brass lump, misshapen from the impact it had made with my chest.
I couldn't help but start laughing, the absurdity of the situation set me almost into hysterics and I stood up, looking back at the police officers who were staring at me with confusion and horror.
" I think this is yours, mate." I beamed, holding up the bullet.

question: You're reading an interplanetary biologist's note book. Describe one of the creatures he observed.
answer:
" Ah, now this is an interesting creature. Upon discovery, twenty-five years ago, I gave them a working name of Exukrell. They were relatively unremarkable, scaled monkey-looking creatures with five prehensile eight-fingered limbs, a prehensile tail, and a second tail that was apparently its natural weapon. Rest in peace Exploro-Bot 243. Shortly thereafter, I left to explore the planet that I called Jennat Azrug. Beautifully blue foliage everywhere, lovely place for a vacation. I'm sure you've seen the movies. Bit of a dramatization but lovely nonetheless. Anyway, I returned to this planet afterwards because I felt there was much yet to be discovered. To my surprise I discovered that the Exukrell had a quite odd natural trait which causes very rapid evolution. They have a short lifespan, incredibly fast reproduction, and highly-mutable DNA. When I returned, they were entirely different creatures. They now had six limbs, four of which were prehensile, the two foremost bearing four talons each, one opposible, the two central bearing five digits, four of them in opposing pairs, and the posterior pair being muscular and able to transport the beast at a surprising rate of speed, though for a limited duration. What's more, they had what appeared to be vestigal wings, to imply that in my 20 year absence, they had evolved to completely different creatures not once, but nearly a full twice! Amazing. Now, five years later, I am already observing new traits in the population I have in captivity. They appear to be modifying their digestive system, and I am excited to see what happens."
I set the notebook down. Well. That must be why this lab looks like it melted.

question: You have lived your entire life seeing colour, but then you meet one person who appears in black and white monochrome. It is that same person who sees only in black and white but sees only you in colour.
answer:
A hand grabs your arm and you whip around, your eyes bulging at the sight of a monochromatic man who looks at you expectantly. The man before you blinks, his eyes wandering to the space around you but what catches your eyes is the grayness spreading from the space the man occupies.

question: This was the worst part of being a double agent.
answer:
Sitting at my desk I popped open the laptop. I'd spent the last five hours in a dark almost abandoned hotel in the seedy underbelly of the only major city in a third world country. I lied, I cheated, I stole. I told people who trusted me with their lives that I was their friend. When they turned around, I shot them in the back. The intel I'd brought in, and the prisoners I'd captured would save countless lives amongst my country's fighting men and women. Even knowing that it was hard to watch someone I'd just said I loved bleed out on the carpet. Her dark red essence seeped into the brown and orange carpet and her eyes pleaded with me not to leave. To stay with her. The noise she made was awkward, rattling, and deeply unsettling. I stepped over her and closed the door on my way out.
That had been three hours ago. Since then, I'd arrived at the embassy. Been debriefed by my handler, and had a coffee in my office at the Ops center. Now I had to write this god damned report. Truly, the paperwork is the worst part of being a double agent.

answer:

answer:
The gentle *ding* that came from the computer made me rub my hands in anticipation. I loved that sound. As fast as humanly possible, my hand whipped out for the mouse so I could open the message.
THE NEW CENSUSES HAVE ARRIVED. PLEASE DOWNLOAD RESULTS AND ADJUST. 
" Martha!" I called for my secretary. She walked through my door and asked, " Yes Sir? Is there anything I can do for you?"
" Why yes you can! I want you to open a line to Minsters of Toxicology, Criminal Corrections, and Anatomy. Please hurry, we will have to edit our current regulations." Martha nodded and started to walk out, but I called after her. " Oh, I'm so excited." A small giggle escaped my mouth. " You know what? You can take the rest of the day off after you patch the Minsters through. Go enjoy yourself, on me." I slid my ID card through my computer and transferred some credits to her account. When her phone buzzed, she smiled and left.
Already, I was pouring over the population spreadsheets. *The large cities are pretty much the same, what a shame. There seems to have been a burst in the rural communities though, too good of a crop season. * I took down notes of possible actions, when I noticed something.
The gender bars were nearly exactly equal in their numbers. Quickly, I looked back to my actions five years ago, and realized that it had been a boy year. I quickly scribbled down a note. *Slash female population by ten percent. *
Just then my computer beeped again and three faces appeared. " Well Gentlemen." I greeted them. " Let's get to work."

question: The origin of the universe is literally a secret. If no one believes the secret the universe ends. The secret bearer is 80 and having trouble finding someone who'll believe it.
answer:
It was my last hope.
" Our next caller is Rutherford from West Virginia. Rutherford, welcome to the Alex Jones show."
Pitiful, isn't it? But I still had family, friends, all of that. I had a reason for doing what I did.
" Alex, I wanted to know: Why don't you ever talk about the Eggs?"
" Eggs, Rutherford?"
" Not just eggs. The Eggs. The ones from which the universe, the stars, and the planets were all formed. Billions of years ago, the Great Mother Hen laid a clutch of Eggs that became everything around us." How long was he going to give me?
" Rutherford, I'll have to admit I haven't heard of the Great Mother Hen before. But we like to keep an open mind at the Alex Jones show."
" The Cosmic Fox is coming, Alex. As long as we believe in the Great Mother Hen, as long as we watch for the Cosmic Fox, he'll stay away. But when the last of the Watchers falls asleep, we're doomed. He'll eat the Eggs."
" Fascinating, Rutherford. That's all the time we have." I heard a click and a dial tone.
It was only a couple of weeks before my family had moved me to an assisted living facility. I didn't complain. Every now and then I would ask a nurse to look for " Great Mother Hen" and " Cosmic Fox" on the Internet. I'd always get a wry smile and a condescending, " Of course I'll help you with that, sir." But I could see the number of Watchers growing, and it gave me peace.

question: You return from the store to find a Dear John letter on the counter.
answer:
I stepped back inside the house, heroically carrying all 6 bags of shopping in one mighty trip.
Setting them down on the kitchen floor and yelling for my wife to come admire my carrying prowess and semi muscular form, I click the kettle on for a well deserved cuppa, taking my mug from the cupboard and placing it on the counter when something catches my eye. There, sitting propped against the toaster is an unmarked, sealed envelope.
Nerves grip me as I rip it open and start scanning the lines...
It's not working...
I need some time...
Terrible in bed...
It's not you, it's me...
I'll always love you in my own way...
Tears fill my eyes as I contemplate my life without her. My first mate on this ship of life. How could I possibly carry on for a single day without knowing she was right here with me? How could I ever manag.. Wait a minute.
My eyes scan to the top of the page and take in the first two words again, properly this time. I laugh and shrug my shoulders as I put my mug away and grab a beer from the fridge instead. I crumple the letter and throw it in the bin without touching the rim. Nailed it, of course.
" Dear John" Indeed.
My name isn't John.

question: After WWIII people have finally realised that war is a human necessity. Every 50 years countries form alliances and different factions declare war to each other. Mass destruction weapons are not allowed. The winners rule the world economy.
answer:
It turns out that war was the only solution that provided stability and preserved freedom. As populations grew, resources became stretched, the envionment neared collapsing. Attempts at forced population control measures only triggered revolutions, and governments were forced to implement draconian control measures to contain them or be destroyed. The situation lead to widespread outbreaks of terrorism, causing further economic chaos and straining resources further. Meanwhille, while humanity dithered, the ice caps began to melt, triggering widespread population migrations and refugee crises. A solution was finally proposed in order to save the human race, and after much debate, adopted by the United Nations.
Every generation, a great war would be called to cull the population. Each nation would call for volunteers to form an army. The nations would then form factions and alliances along idealogical lines, and prepare their forces. They would be landed on the shores of Antartica, and then, at a pre-determined time, march for the South Pole. The war lasted until the worlds population had been reduced by 10 %, with whichever faction controlled the pole at the time being granted control of the United Nations Security Council until the next war.

question: In the future, online gaming etiquette is recorded and a mandatory part of background checks when applying or interviewing for jobs.
answer:
As he ran a finger down the sheaf of paper stacked before him, my interviewer made a harumphing sound, his lower lip jutting forward. He blew air up through his fluffy black mustache.
" Well," he said, " I must admit, Mr. Fields, this is quite a rap sheet."
I shifted. The chair was too small, and too close to the floor -- my legs were falling asleep just sitting here.
" I've had counseling," I offered. " I know my past is rocky, but I've made a turn for the better. I'm a new man."
" Yes, but -- quite a rap sheet, indeed."
" Is there anything in particular you would like to discuss?"
" Well, it seems you wished cancer upon other human beings not once, or twice, but actually eleven hundred times."
" We all make mistakes."
" Looks like your favorite insult, used five thousand times in Dota 2 over a three year period, was'shitscuttling dickbuffet."'
I was actually quite proud to have come up with that one.
" Hmm," I said.
" Now, Mr. Fields, is someone who says'shitscuttling dickbuffet' more frequently than any other phrase *really* the kind of person who is going to fit in with the culture here at Adams, Adams & Adams?"
" I think part of what makes Adams, Adams & Adams the place I want to work is the ability of its employees to laugh at themselves," I ventured. " In that respect I think yes, while it might be a bit coarse, the phrase also demonstrates a degree of humor and creativity that could make me an excellent fit."
My interviewer remained unconvinced, his mustache drooping doubtfully.
" I see," he said, tapping the stack of paper with a knobby finger.

" No, what?"
" How did you come here?"

" What?"
" I've dreamt about you like four times before for the past two weeks. But this is the first time you've seen me. And talked to me."
" You.. Is your name Sarah Conner?"
" Yes, how'd you know that?"
" Fuck."

question: You are an indigenous tribesman. You have never left the forest or come into contact with any advanced society. You climb a mountain, searching for glory, and you come across a modern city, the likes of which you have never seem before. Describe the city from your perspective
answer:
A million stars that have fallen to the plains lay before my eyes. Everything which I have heard of now speaks its truth in this very moment. The light of the gods, dancing over the hills, arranging themselves as trees with the height of mountains. The sky above, a mixture of night and day. The shadows of rigid birds that never stopped flying. The sounds of angry bulls that never stopped growling.
Every grounded star acted as one of the sun's children, trying to light the sky but still falling short of mother moon, whose face was full and round tonight. Some were moving. Others stayed still. Some were cold, glowing the color of winter ice. Others burned fiery anger. Still others were neutral in their demeanor, as if to suggest their wisdom in being even tempered.
To both sides, smaller stars decorated shorter trees. It was as if they were the witchdoctors of the star tribe, preferring solitude to the loud campfire the other stars gathered around. Their message was unclear though. For what reason would they travel from the sky, only to sit so far from their neighbors?
The smoke of a million fires surly found its way to my senses, as my father told me would happen. I coughed, and my chest ached for the earth. These were not dutiful gods who cared for the earth, they were shameful gods who seek to live the lives of their human offspring.

question: " Words are like weapons that must be taken away. "
answer:
Decades after the written language had been established in Sumeria, the following inscription was found on a large stela in a temple courtyard.
By leading us astray you have destroyed the Image and the Image came before the Word. The Word came afterwards in an attempt to describe the Image to those who had not been able to envision in themselves. This is where the illusion began.
The Image must be reinstated and It can only exist through it's re-creation by visualization. Through the use of useless words you have caused the Image to melt away, to vanish into nothingness; and the vacuum created thereby has been filled with a false image. The false image has set many on the wrong path; the illusion is a tempting path to follow.
Words are material representations of images and can never replace the Image itself so it is thereby dangerous, sinful and illusory to try to use them for any purpose. Turn off the word mill in your mind for it grinds a bitter powder out of the seeds of illusion. Think in pictures and speak not so that the Image will be restored and consciousness will be put back on the path of Truth.

question: Begin or end a story with: " She smiles. 'I've been waiting for you. ' "
answer:
She smiles. " I've been waiting for you."
She speaks, and shortly I nod my head slowly, yet I keep my eyes on her. " I've watched you for so long, wondering when this moment will come," she says. I stand there, watching her walk-, no, glide towards me, as if she had all the time in the world. As she approaches, I shiver. " And now that it has, I feel elated," she speaks down to a whisper. She gets even closer, but doesn't quite touch me. I try to move, but the moment is taking over me. Maybe it already has. I try to speak, yet I realize that there are no words to say.
I look into her eye, knowing exactly who she was. The truth is, I've been longing for her too, for a long time. She knows. Yet I didn't make an effort to meet her. Someone had to do it for me, and though I do want to see her, now is not the time.
" Are you ready?" she asks. I nod, or try to, but before I could, she kisses me, and I fall down on my knees. As I fall towards the ground, I see her moving towards someone else. I hit the floor, lying beside the others. Slowly, darkness and cold covers me, and the last thing I hear is her voice.
I can see, even through the darkness.
She smiles. " I've been waiting for you."

question: They watched us. They waited. Time is over. They are coming.
answer:
We ran. We ran far and wide as far as we could. We were given so little warning, so little time to flee.
IT was coming for us. We hid.
Some sought refuge in nature, choosing to hide amongst the trees at the edges of our world. Others hid beneath the edifices of civilization, structures built long before our generation's birth for little more than the purpose of our amusement. How strange that we would cower in the shade they offered, whispering secrets and rumors to each other about... IT.
Finally our time was up. We heard the last moments of the countdown and then watched silently as IT came into our midst, prepared to seek and give chase to each of us in turn. We quelled in terror, wondering which unlucky bastard would be first to be found, first to be turned, twisted, *changed* by the mere touch of IT.
IT turned its dread face towards us as we cowered just out of sight, barely suppressing panic into anxiety, and then IT opened that horrible maw and screamed at us those horrible words,
" READY OR NOT HERE I COME!"
But then the bell rang and we had to go back inside.

question: You have wandered the galaxies for many, many years; you've met with other wanderers in a discussion forum, and the ONE common observation is that all systems with habitats suitable to humankind also have at least one ringed planet. [ WP ]
answer:
" Uh... Jim?"
" Damnit, what is it now? More space monsters?"
Jim Turpin floated in the capsule, checking numbers on the data readouts. Behind him, Jules O'Connor flipped through a notebook.
" No! Just... you ever look at the Systems?"
" Yeah, every damn day. What's the read on the TTPV?"
" 40-5.56. No, I mean... Sol has Saturn, Archaea has Typhon, Akatsuki has Izanami- all these systems, the ones we live in... they have ringed planets."
"... Right."
" No, seriously! I checked the list, and there's not one without a ringed planet. Not one."
" Jules, algorithms can be faulty-"
" By hand."
That quieted Jim. "... Alright, so what do you think?"
" I don't know what to think."
There was silence in the capsule for a few minutes, and then Jim produced his tablet, flipping through listings.
" B-33432-Alpha. Ringed planet. TT-59006-Kappa. Ringed planet..." He continued, examining each and every noted system on the list rated for human life.
Ringed planets. All of them.
" Wha... Jules?"
" Yeah?"
"... I don't like this."
" Neither do I. But..."
" But?"
" We could use DeepScan."
" That's not rated for gas giants."
" At worst we get a negative."
Jim watched Jules for a minute, before nodding. In one hour, the ship was in orbit around Hades. In two, they had a result.
And they wished they didn't.

question: A man is doomed to repeat the last 2014 seconds of Dec. 31st unless he meets some random and mundane condition.
answer:
" I can't take it anymore!" he shouted in desperation. " What do I have to do? Throw those petunias off the roof? Will that make it stop?" He had been yelling to no one in particular for the past few minutes.
The distraught man marched to a pot of petunias, and launched it from his 22 story apartment window.
Then the countdown came. The man began sobbing into his hands as he neared what had to have been the one hundred and seventy eighth iteration of the minutes prior to New Years Eve. He didn't know why, but time was repeating, and only he seemed to notice.
" 3..2... 1... Happy New Year!" He heard from his window.
He stood up, a shocked expression on his face. " Huh? But time didn't go back." he said sheepishly.
" Must've been the petunias," his couch replied.

question: In 2560, artificial intelligence has matched human intelligence. Humans coexist with robots that look and behave identically to humans. There is only one question that can expose whether somebody is a robot, and you ask it to the most important person in your life.
answer:
My father and I were out fishing, it was good to get away from the busy buzz of the city. And not to sound bigoted, but occasionally the robots creeped me out a little too. I mean a couple of my friends were robots; it should just be normal by now, but for some reason it wasn't. What if a few of the people I thought I knew were actually robots?
" Earth to John, Earth to John." My father repeated while he waved his hand in front of my face, " You seem kinda lost in your thoughts there."
" Yeah," I replied with a sigh, " I'm just thinking about robots again, is all"
He chuckled and patted me on the back, " don't worry about all that, it's just you and me out here."
I let my thoughts sift around for a while as the boat rocked back and forth. An idea sprang to me.
" Hey dad" I said, " What's one tenth plus two tenths?"
" 0.30000000000000004" He answered. In one instant, his eyes shot open, he covered his mouth, and his skin paled. Fucking busted.
____
If you don't get it:
Computers process things in binary. In binary, 1/10 and 2/10 are repeating decimals (like how 1/3 =.33333) so there is a tiny bit of error when computing with them.

He chuckled to himself again. *Ah, Jenna. You and I will never forget today, * he laughed inwardly. Though, she was a forgetful person. It'd be just like her to forget her date with him again.

question: Write a story that involves blood, but reminds you of home.
answer: The first time I saw a cow give birth was while standing outside the barn on a cool April day as grey as they come in rural Manitoba. I had been wandering around the barnyard, as I often did, with a walking stick imagining I was a powerful sorcerer or slave pit fighter just managing to survive my next encounter in the arena. As I turned around the corner of our old bowed in barn I saw one of our cows laying on her stomach slightly to the side. Something in my mind knew that this moment was an important one as I stopped dead in my tracks to stare. I stood there silently for a half hour watching this cow give birth, cheering her on in my mind. Until finally, with one final push a slimy calf was born into the world. Within seconds it was hobbling up onto it's bony legs to wander around it's exhausted mother. The sense of beauty at what I had just witnessed was exhilarating.

question:
In a round-robin scheduler, adding a process multiple times to the process list is a cheap way to give it higher priority.

I wonder how practical an approach this might be. What benefit does it have over other techniques such as giving the process a longer time slice (benefit: less switching time) or maintaining a separate list of high-priority processes. In particular, how does listing a process multiple times influence fairness and reactivity?

(From exercise 2.16 in Andrew Tanenbaum's Operating Systems: Design and Implementation 1st ed.)
answer:
The advantage of this approach is that round robin scheduling is very efficient, so you don't need to rely on a more complex scheduler, which would steal cycles. Introducing longer time slices for higher priority processes would decrease the responsiveness of other threads and make it harder for the OS to jump in to deal with an interrupt and so forth. Maintaining separate lists of processes would require a much more complex scheduler, which would be more expensive in terms of cycles. I don't see how there would be any problem with fairness, though. I guess the problem is that the granularity is fairly course: processes can only have integer multiples of the basic time-slice.

One negative point is that removing a process would be more costly, as each occurrence of the process would have to be removed from the queue. Perhaps this can be done lazily, though.

question: I am taking a complexity course and I am having trouble with coming up with reductions between NPC problems. How can I find reductions between problems? Is there a general trick that I can use? How should I approach a problem that asks me to prove a problem is NPC?
answer:
JeffE outlines the most common strategy: know lots of NP-complete problems, find one that fits very well and make the easy reduction.

Another valid strategy is to always use 3SAT (or any other problem). This might make some reductions more intricate, but the upside is that you have lots of experience expressing satifiability in other types of problems. So you save the time of finding a good reduction partner (including dead-ends) and hope that your experience will allow you to do the reduction quickly even if it is harder.

This approach has some meta beauty, too: (3)SAT is one of the few problems for which NP-completeness has been proven (almost) directly. Therefore, relying only on that proof keeps your "proof tree" flat, avoiding long chains of reductions.

question:
Why do you think it is that most C++ instructors teaching college level computer sciences discourage or even forbid using strings for text, instead requiring students to use character arrays?

I am assuming this methodology is somehow intended to teach good programming habits, but in my experience I don't see anything wrong with just using strings, and they are significantly easier to use and learn.
answer:
Koenig and Moe's Accelerated C++ and Stroustrup's Programming: Principles and Practice Using C++ are using std::string and other components from the standard library from the start. If I remember correctly, they don't even present C arrays for Koenig and Moe and Stroustrup does it quite late in the book (perhaps even just in an annex).

That approach, qualified as modern, is the preferred one in my circles. The other approach, often qualified as historic, follows more closely how C++ evolved, but doesn't take advantage of "newer" (relatively, they are 15 years old now) development and doesn't teach what is practised now (at least on projects not encumbered with too much legacy) but 10 years ago (there is always a lag before being mainstream).

question: Dynamic programming can reduce the time needed to perform a recursive algorithm. I know that dynamic programming can help reduce the time complexity of algorithms. Are the general conditions such that if satisfied by a recursive algorithm would imply that using dynamic programming will reduce the time complexity of the algorithm? When should I use dynamic programming?
answer:
Dynamic programming is useful is your recursive algorithm finds itself reaching the same situations (input parameters) many times. There is a general transformation from recursive algorithms to dynamic programming known as memoization, in which there is a table storing all results ever calculated by your recursive procedure. When the recursive procedure is called on a set of inputs which were already used, the results are just fetched from the table. This reduces recursive Fibonacci to iterative Fibonacci.

Dynamic programming can be even smarter, applying more specific optimizations. For example, sometimes there is no need to store the entire table in memory at any given time.

question:
I've come across many definitions of recursive and recursively enumerable languages. But I couldn't quite understand what they are .

Can some one please tell me what they are in simple words?
answer:
Not really. You should read a few books. Perhaps we can recommend some.

That said, a language is recursive if there is a Turing machine than can always reply "yes" or "no" if a given string is part of this language. If we lift this requirement to merely say "yes" for strings of the language (it can run forever if it is not) then we have a recursively enumerable language. It is not hard to see, that a recursive language can be decided by a Turing machine, while a recursively enumerable language can have its strings listed (for example, by running an infinite number of Turing machines in parallel — yes this is possible, see dove-tailing — on all strings of the alphabet, and outputting a string if the corresponding TM accepts). There are many, many equivalent definitions.

question:
Let's say we have a fictional operating system in the user mode. Whenever an interrupt or a trap occurs, the os would switch to the Kernel mode jumping to the address determined from the interrupt vector. A malicious user could take advantage of the loophole by executing a malicious program in the kernel mode.

Why is it dangerous ? What could have the user possibly done to achieve this and what kind of remedy would you suggest for the loop hole ?
answer:
The malicious user has to first get the malicious code into kernel space somehow. User and kernel address spaces often look contiguous under linux and various unixes, but user space isn't mapped into kernel space, and vice versa. Some variations of Unix (the Masscomp system, as I recall) made this more explicit by having user space and kernel space start at 0x00000000. So, that's the first problem: code at 0x0804890c (or where ever) writeable by the user doesn't exist in the kernel's address space.

Secondly, the malicious user would have to have the ability to change the interrupt vector. This vector conceptually could live in either kernel or user space, but probably resides in kernel space. If the interrupt vector resides in kernel space, the user doesn't have write access. If the interrupt vector resides in user space, it's marked read-only, and the addresses in it point to code in kernel space. Which is why problem (1) above for the malicious user exists.

I am an electrical engineer, and only had one CS course in college 26 years ago. However, I am also a devoted Mathematica user.

I have the sense that Turing Machines are very important in computer science. Is the importance only in the theory of computer science? If there are practical implications/applications what are some of them?
answer:
The importance of Turing machines is twofold. First, Turing machines were one of the first (if not the first) theoretical models for computers, dating from 1936. Second, a lot of theoretical computer science has been developed with Turing machines in mind, and so a lot of the basic results are in the language of Turing machines. One reason for this is that Turing machines are simple, and so amenable to analysis.

That said, Turing machines are not a practical model for computing. As an engineer and a Mathematica user, they shouldn't concern you at all. Even in the theoretical computer science community, the more realistic RAM machines are used in the areas of algorithms and data structures.

In fact, from the point of view of complexity theory, Turing machines are polynomially equivalent to many other machine models, and so complexity classes like P and NP can equivalently be defined in terms of these models. (Other complexity classes are more delicate.)

I was reading about Universal Turing Machines.

I see that the matching lemma states, that between two symbols X and Y, if there are only 1-s and blanks, then a TM exists, which can count the number of ones.

Now I wonder, would there also be a TM or a method of implementation of a TM which can match two strings? To me it intuitively appears, that inifinitely many symbols implies infinitely many states for the machine, and an example workflow may look like: found symbol X, enter state stateX, exit stateX to state readnextchar if again X was found on the second tape.

Would that not mean an infinitely long transition table? or is there an way to represent a table in a smaller way?

if the symbols are represented via some kind of place value system, e.g. decimal, binary, would that shorten the transition table length?
answer:
Turing machines can simulate whatever algorithm you can actually program. So if you can solve your problem by writing a program in C or python (for example), then a Turing machine can also solve your problem.

The most general statement of this principle - everything that is computable can be computed using a Turing machine - is known as the Church-Turing hypothesis. For the specific case of languages like C or python, we know that this hypothesis is true - in principle you can convert every program in C or python to an equivalent Turing machine. The Turing machine would be a lot slower, though. (But only by a polynomial amount!)

For your specific problem, you can allocate a specific location in the tape for your the variables you need, and then update them as you go. The number of states in the Turing machine is proportional (more or less) to the number of instructions in assembly code for your algorithm. Actually programming Turing machines is hard and somewhat pointless. Memory handling is particularly awkward, but Turing machines can implement arrays, tables, and other data structures by allocating special areas on the tape and maintaining them. Perhaps you will hear more about that later in your class.

Finally, for the reason you mention, the tape alphabet is always finite. Without loss of generality, we can assume that it contains only zero and one, though that might make programming the Turing machine even harder. Data structures such as strings and numbers can be encoded in just the same way that they are encoded in your computer - as a string of zeroes and ones.

Without loss of generality, we can assume that it contains only zero and one, though that might make programming the Turing machine even harder. question:
If I am right students learning computer science at universities learn very theoretical kind of knowledge. A knowledge most of which (e.g. algorithm theory) can't be used to create everyday software (e.g. MS Word, IE, etc.).

What opportunities do computer science graduates have if they don't want to do research but rather work at some company where they can make use of what they have studied. (e.g. not writing MS Word)

In case of still not being clear enough, generally speaking, what I would like to know is what can a computer science gradute work?
answer:
You are just wrong.

First of all I would hope that any four-year bachelor's degree (in any major) would teach basic critical thinking skills, which is really the prerequisite that employers (of any kind) are looking for.

Second of all I don't think you understand what software engineers actually do. (They design algorithms to solve real problems, and then make sure that the algorithms are implemented in reusable, testable, and composable ways.) I guarantee that majority of the programmers who work on the IE and MS Word teams have at least an undergraduate degree in computer science, and use something they learned in that degree every day.

Third of all, I don't think you understand what computer science programs actually teach. A computer science degree involves a lot more than a single course on complexity theory and a single course on computability theory. It involves dozens of courses all aimed at helping the student think algorithmically. All the computer science programs I've been associated with have required significant amounts of basic mathematics (calculus, statistics, linear algebra, analysis), and also things like digital, computer, operating system, database, networking, and compiler design. (And algorithm design.) Also linear programming, numerical analysis, signal and image processing, cryptography, machine learning, graphics.

I would never hire someone who didn't understand algorithms and complexity theory to write software (even web apps). (Or more accurately: I would hire just about any clear thinker to write software, but if they didn't already know how to design algorithms I would realize that I was going to have to invest a substantial amount of time and money teaching them to design algorithms.)

question:
I'm a bit confused about these concepts. As far as I understand, something is Turing complete when it can simulate a Turing machine. And there is this thing called a Universal Turing machine which is universal because it can simulate a Turing machine. Which to me, implies there are Turing machines that are not universal and cannot simulate a Turing machine. Does this mean non-universal Turing machines are not Turing complete?

Could anyone clarify this concepts for me?
answer:
In short yes, a non-universal Turing Machine is not Turing-complete.

The key part is that a computational model is Turing-complete if it can simulate any Turing Machine (or using the transitivity of the simulations, if it can simulate a Universal Turing Machine).

As you note, many Turing Machines are not Universal, they compute something, but they can't simulate any computation that any Turing Machine could do.

A possibly intuitive practical way of thinking about this is that Turing Machines are normally equivalent to programs - they take a particular type of input and compute some output. Universal Turing Machines are equivalent to programming languages or computers - you can build/run any program/Turing Machine on them. Of course I'm using "equivalent" very loosely here.

question: Since buying computation power is much affordable than in the past, are the knowledge of algorithms and being efficient getting less important? It's clear that you would want to avoid an infinite loop, so, not everything goes. But if you have better hardware, could you have somehow worse software?
answer:
On the contrary. At the same time that hardware is getting cheaper, several other developments take place.

First, the amount of data to be processed is growing exponentially. This has led to the study of quasilinear time algorithms, and the area of big data. Think for example about search engines - they have to handle large volumes of queries, process large amounts of data, and do it quickly. Algorithms are more important than ever.

Second, the area of machine learning is growing strong, and full of algorithms (albeit of a different kind than what you learn in your BA). The area is thriving, and every so often a truly new algorithm is invented, and improves performance significantly.

Third, distributed algorithms have become more important, since we are hitting a roadblock in increasing CPU processing speed. Nowadays computing power is being increased by parallelizing, and that involves dedicated algorithms.

Fourth, to counterbalance the increasing power of CPUs, modern programming paradigms employ virtual machine methods to combat security loopholes. That slows these programs down by an appreciable factor. Adding to the conundrum, your operating system is investing more CPU time on bells and whistles, leaving less CPU time for your actual programs, which could include CPU-intensive algorithms such as video compression and decompression. So while hardware is faster, it's not used as efficiently.

Summarizing, efficient algorithms are necessary to handle large amounts of data; new kinds of algorithms are popping up in the area of artificial intelligence; distributed algorithms are coming into focus; and CPU power is harnessed less efficiently for various reasons (but mainly, because computers are getting more powerful). Algorithms are not dead yet.

First and foremost, i know what a shell, kernel is. Now the dilemma.

Today i had my systems viva in college. The examiner asked me is there a shell between the hardware and the kernel. Obviously, i said no, and the gave the usual explanation that the shell is an interpreter, it takes the user input, interprets the command and communicates with the kernel via system calls.

answer:

It is likely that either there was some misunderstanding or that the examiner is confused. The former is much, much more likely.

One thing I might critique is your characterization of a shell as an interpreter. While a shell is an interpreter, not every interpreter is a shell. I suppose it is possible that the examiner was asking a follow-up question to see if you understand that.

As far as how a kernel runs programs.... read a standard operating system textbook. The details are adequately covered in any standard OS textbook.

The thing is... I'm not sure why you're asking us. Why not ask your professor or examiner? We can't tell you what was in your examiner's head.

question:
What is a good metaphor or example to explain to an English major the difference between classical computer science and "being good with using MS-Windows"

computer science

computer programming

using computers

3 profoundly different things. Most people have no idea what Computer Science even is. They just see the word "computer". Hence, "he is a Computer Science major" can be interpreted as "He can hook up my printer". Or that he's "good with computers". Even fewer people know the difference between computer programming and Computer Science.

Computer Science is computing theory. CS can be learned without actual computers. CPU micro architecture. How to sort numbers, how to traverse lists, etc. State machines. Algorithms, big(Oh), etc. How to design a programming language or compiler.

Programming is writing code and creating applications in a language and compiler created by a computer scientist.

Lastly, there is using a computer (using a GUI, mouse, and keyboard. Internet, MS-Office, etc)

Yet all three of these are used interchangeably by laymen.

What is a good metaphor or example to explain to an English major the difference between classical computer science and "being good with using MS-Windows" Or simply, a pithy example of how real computer science has nothing to do with using MS-Windows.
answer:
How about an automotive analogy?

uses computers and maybe "is good with computers" :: a driver (can drive and refuel safely) and maybe a car enthusiast (can jump start a car; is familiar with many makes and models; knows techniques like using windshield treatment to keep rain from reducing visibility).

programmer :: an automotive mechanic or technician. Knows how cars work. Can repair and modify cars and even build kit cars. Ought to know how to debug/diagnose problems by using the scientific method. Might not be aware of relevant theory and thus might write O(n2) loops.

software engineer :: an automotive engineer. Designs cars, engines, and other components that you can entrust your life with, and does it within schedule, cost, manufacturability, and other constraints. Knows how to apply the relevant theory/math such as finite element analysis.

computer scientist :: an automotive scientist. Researches new ideas in vehicles, human-machine interfaces, and propulsion. Does computational crash test modeling. Adds to the body of theory and experimental results.

So for people who equate all “computing” with “proficient in using some software package,” that's like equating driving proficiency with the ability to design antilock brakes that we trust lives to, that are manufacturable with consistent high quality and low cost, and work for years in extreme weather. Or equating driving proficiency with researching what kind of radar-triggered braking features will avoid collisions without freaking the driver into swerving into another lane.

Perhaps lay people confuse these terms because "computer science" classes teach computer use skills, programming, theory, or engineering. All that stuff (arguably not the first part) fits in the curriculum of computer science. None of it is the end-all "content" of computer science, just as English classes are learning on the way to an English major (a fuzzier concept).

question: Which one is better approach do data compression before encrypting it or Encrypt data before compression ? I think it is biased towards the application requirement. Please share your views.
answer:
Always compress first. The goal of encryption is to make data look random and it's impossible to compress random data. Therefore, if you succeed in significantly compressing encrypted data, you need to look for a new encryption algorithm.

If encrypted data doesn't look random, that's a big hint about how to decrypt it. For example, substitution cyphers fail because (assuming the plaintext is ordinary English prose and it's reasonably long) the most common character is almost certain to be the code for E. The next most common characters are almost certain to be the codes for T, A, O and so on.

question: I've always wondered why processors stopped at 32 registers. It's by far the fastest piece of the machine, why not just make bigger processors with more registers? Wouldn't that mean less going to the RAM?
answer:
Just two more reasons for limiting the number of registers:

Little gain to be expected: CPU such as current Intel/AMD x64 models have 32kByte and more of L1-D cache, and access to the L1 cache usually takes only one clock cycle (compared to about a hundred clock cycles for a complete single RAM access). So there is little to be gained from having more data in registers compared to having data in the L1 cache

Additional computational costs: Having more registers creates an overhead that may actually make a computer slower:

In multitasking-environments, a task switch usually has to save the contents of all registers of the process that is left to memory, and has to load those of the process to be entered. The more registers you have, the longer this takes.

Similarly, in architectures without register windows, cascaded function calls use the same set of registers. So a function A calling a function B uses the same set of registers as B itself. Therefore, B has to save the contents of all registers it uses (which still hold A's values) and has to write them back before returning (in some calling conventions it is the job of A to save its register contents before calling B, but the overhead is similar). The more registers you have, the longer does this saving take, and thus the more expensive a function call becomes.

question: On the matter of the Heartbleed bug, Bruce Schneier wrote in his Crypto-Gram of 15th April: '"Catastrophic" is the right word. On the scale of 1 to 10, this is an 11.' I read several years ago that a kernel of a certain operating system has been rigorously verified with a modern program verification system. Could hence bugs of the genre of Heartbleed be prevented from occurring via application of program verification techniques today or is this yet unrealistic or even principally impossible?
answer:
To answer your question in the most concise way - yes, this bug could have potentially been caught by formal verification tools. Indeed, the property "never send a block which is bigger than the size of the hearbeat that was sent" is fairly simple to formalize in most specification languages (e.g. LTL).

The problem (which is a common criticism against formal methods) is that the specifications you use are written by humans. Indeed, formal methods only shift the bug-hunting challenge from finding the bugs to defining what bugs are. This is a difficult task.

Also, formally verifying software is notoriously difficult due to the state-explosion problem. In this case, it is especially relevant, since many times in order to avoid the state explosion, we abstract away bounds. For example, when we want to say "every request is followed by a grant, within 100000 steps", we need a very long formula, so we abstract it to the formula "every request is eventually followed by a grant".

Thus, in the heartbleed case, even while attempting to formalize the requirements, the bound in question could have been abstracted away, resulting in the same behavior.

To sum up, potentially this bug could have been avoided by using formal methods, but there would have had to be a human specifying this property in advance.

question:
I am confused between these two terminologies: recursively enumerable language, recursively enumerable set.

Do they have the exactly same meaning?
answer:
No they do not have exactly the same meaning. A language is a set of strings, whereas a set can be virtually anything. Usually such a set is a set of (natural) numbers, but we also can consider sets of graphs.

However, when the sets are accepted or generated by Turing machines, then they have to be represented on a tape (for input or output). This means they have to be represented as strings anyhow. Hence for the Turing machine itself there is no difference. Only for the human beholder there is an interpretation of the string as number or graph.

question:
I'm writing a research paper and I have to basically say that one microcontroller is slower than an other microprocessor. However, I'm worried that simply saying that it's 'slower' wouldn't be appropriate in a research paper.

Am I right? Is it OK to just say that one processor is 'slower', or do I need to say something else? What else could I say? The best I have come up with is that one has 'less computational power' than the other or that the microcontroller has 'low computational power'. Unfortunately, these expressions don't seem to be too popular when searching online.

So, what would be a better and academically correct way of saying this?
answer:
Claiming that a microprocessor has a "speed" is very, very difficult nowadays.

You can look at the clock rate, which is mostly a meaningless number nowadays. Especially since microprocessors don't have one clock rate anymore, but run at varying speeds depending on many circumstances. You can look at the number of cores, which is also meaningless if we don't know how many cores the application can use. You can look at the computer architecture, and rely on claims of the manufacturers of speed. The computer's memory can have different speeds. If it doesn't have enough memory, the operating system starts swapping memory which takes time.

If you said "this microprocessor is slower", without some reasoning why it is slower for the application you are interested in, I would be dubious and think you might not know what you are talking about. If you said "it has less computational power" I'd think you are trying to bluff your way through the paper. If you called it "less performant" as was suggested, all doubts on my side would be gone.

Write down in your paper which microprocessor models you are comparing (they all have exact names so anyone interested can look up the details anyway), give all the relevant specs (architecture, clock speed, number of cores, amount of L1, L2 and L3 cache), and explain why one is slower for the purpose you are discussing, based on this data.

As you noted, for crippled Turing machines, using unary and binary encoded numbers would not yield an equivalent model of computation.

So I was thinking about how garbage collectors work and I thought of an interesting issue. Presumably garbage collectors have to traverse all structures in the same way. They can't know weather they are traversing a linked list or a balanced tree or whatever. They also can't use up too much memory in their search. One possible way, and the only way I can think to traverse ALL structures, might be just to traverse them all recursively the way you would a binary tree. This however would give a stack overflow on a linked list or even just a poorly balanced binary tree. But all the garbage collected languages that I have ever used seem to have no problem dealing with such cases.

In the dragon book it uses a "Unscanned" queue of sorts. Basically rather than traversing the structure recursively it just adds things that need to be marked too a queue and then for each thing not marked at the end it is deleted. But wouldn't this queue get very large?

So, how do garbage collectors traverse arbitrary structures? How does this traversal technique avoid overflow?
answer:
Note that I am not a garbage collection expert. This answer only gives examples of techniques. I do not claim that it is a representative overview of garbage collection techniques.

An unscanned queue is a common choice. The queue can get large — potentially as large as the deepest data structure. The queue is typically stored explicitly, not on the stack of the garbage collection thread.

Once all but one of the children of a node have been scanned, the node can be removed from the unscanned queue. This is basically a tail call optimization. Garbage collectors can include heuristics to attempt to scan the deepest child of a node last; for example a GC for Lisp should scan the car of a cons before the cdr.

One way to avoid keeping an unscanned queue is to modify pointers in place, making the child temporarily point to the parent. This is a constant-memory tree traversal technique that's used in contexts other than garbage collectors. The downside of this technique is that while the GC is traversing a data structure, the data structure is invalid, so the GC has to stop the world. This isn't a deal breaker: many garbage collectors do include a phase that stops the world, in addition to phases that don't but can miss garbage as a result.
